subtopic: POLICY ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING FEED GRAINS IN EASTERN CANADA
POLICY ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING FEED GRAINS IN EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I have the pleasure of announcing to the house that the government has authorized an interim policy on feed grains. Henceforth western grain moved by trucks within eastern Canada will also be eligible for freight assistance. Moreover, the government has decided on a new basis for the payment of freight assistance.
These two reforms were necessary. The original policy goes back to 1941. Many changes have occurred since its introduction. Methods and rates of transportation have changed and the fact that freight assistance was available only on inland movement by rail tended to prevent the decrease of certain inland rates. Some inequities in the balance of costs to various destinations have resulted.
We wished to correct these deficiencies immediately in order to follow up the measure concerning reimbursement of winter storage costs in authorized eastern elevators, introduced last autumn by my colleague the Minister of Agriculture. This measure, established simultaneously with the extension to barley and oats of the Canadian wheat board's policy of deferred pricing, encourages a more economical movement of grain during the navigation season, and sufficient stock-piling of grains in the east for winter needs. For this reason eastern prices of grains and millfeeds have fluctuated much less during the last year.
The changes now made should therefore permit the most economical transportation of feed grains to their destination. More active competition will lower a number of rates.
As to its consequences for livestock producers, it can be said that this new policy
will result in substantial reductions in the spread between balances of transportation costs payable by producers in various regions. This spread under the former policy ran from an excess of assistance paid over the actual transportation cost of $1.80 to a balance of cost payable by local producers reaching $6.20 in certain areas. Under this new policy we have sought to narrow this spread of approximately $8 to $2.60 in eastern Canada, and we expect truck competition to eventually reduce it to less than $1.60.
All regions of British Columbia will see their balance of cost reduced by $0.60. Northern Ontario and northwestern Quebec will benefit from reductions reaching up to $3.60. There will be an appreciable reduction at most points north of the St. Lawrence, in various regions of the maritimes farthest from ports of entry and in some zones in Newfoundland. Furthermore, in other regions an effort has been made to standardize balance of cost wherever possible, while ensuring a readjustment for destination points receiving assistance in excess of cost of transportation.
I may say that rates to the maritimes are based on water movement. We plan to keep a close watch on supplies as the season progresses and should stocks in storage in the area be inadequate by the close of navigation, the government is prepared to re-examine the matter.
We repeat that our new policy, which will come into effect on August 31 next, is only an interim policy. We are waiting for the report of the house committee on agriculture and the result of certain studies, before establishing a more permanent feed grain policy.
Moreover such a permanent policy must be coherently integrated with overall legislation aimed at the agricultural renovation of eastern Canada.

subtopic: POLICY ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING FEED GRAINS IN EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Forestry, who is now responsible for the feed grain policy, has just announced a temporary program concerning the transportation of feed grain by truck to eastern Canada. That is a step to help the trucking industry and, indirectly, in a small way, eastern agriculture. But in no way is it what we expected today from the Minister of Forestry.

Grain Policy in Eastern Canada
The Minister of Forestry just said he is waiting for the agriculture committee's report on the feed grain situation before bringing forward a new policy. Now, on May 22 of this year he stated on television that he was waiting for that report before introducing his new policy on feed grain.
Mr. Speaker, last year we asked the government to set up a committee to examine the question of feed grain in eastern Canada. The committee on agriculture met several times to consider the situation. A certain number of people gave very valuable information enabling the government to establish a new policy instead of a political scheme and thus ensuring what we, Conservatives, have sought to realize: stability of supplies, price equalization, encouragement for feed grain production in the east and price stability for feed grain throughout eastern Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is all very well to say that the report of the committee on agriculture is forthcoming, but ever since December 1963 we have repeatedly asked that the committee be reconvened to examine the alarming situation in eastern Canada.
And as things are going, we shall come back to this matter only this fall, in October or November, and once again we shall find ourselves in the same situation as last year. Prices will fluctuate just as they did from August to January 1964, when there was a difference of $8 a ton.
Well, we are not satisfied, even though this statement of interim policy is a step forward; we are not at all satisfied with this announcement and the responsible minister, instead of telling us that he is waiting for the committee report, should force the government to bring pressure to bear on the committee on agriculture to have it submit its report without delay. We are ready. There were always from 15 to 18 members present at this committee, and we intend to see to it that the government gives us the necessary instructions.

subtopic: POLICY ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING FEED GRAINS IN EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we wish to thank the minister for the announcement he made this morning, which I believe was divided into two parts. The first part concerns a change that has been made in the policy previously followed of giving subsidies only to the railroads on the movement of grain inland for feed purposes. There are many areas in which the railroads are not the most efficient means of


transporting grain, and there are other areas solely dependant on road transportation. These areas have not received the benefit of this subsidy.
We believe the policy of extending the subsidy all across Canada is very good. It is one that has been recommended by many members of my party for a number of years because of the disparity which has existed between areas in this country. If this policy is implemented immediately it will eliminate some of thi problems we had last year when storage charges were paid. We found that even in the Ottawa area, which is close to the terminal elevators, the price fluctuated from $5 to $6 during the winter months. In my opinion this new policy eliminates the last reason the feed operators have for making these additional charges.
I believe the minister is completely wrong in the second aspect of his announcement relating to the whole problem of feed grain in eastern Canada. As the previous member has said, the government has shown no interest in having this matter again brought before the agriculture committee. In the committee last year there was general agreement that there should be a marketing agency established similar to the Canadian wheat board which would operate in the eastern feed grain areas. This suggestion was violently opposed by government members, with the result that the committee has not dealt with the problem again.
I think it is wrong to put these two problems together because obviously, in my opinion, they do not mean the same thing. We are now extending to road transport a subsidy that has previously been available only to rail transport. The other problem of eastern feed grain is not going to be solved this easily. It will only be done when the committee gets down to making formal recommendations to which the government can give consideration. I personally hope the government refers this matter to the committee in the very near future.

subtopic: POLICY ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING FEED GRAINS IN EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course, members of the house had been waiting for such a statement from the minister for some time. Personally, I brought up the matter many times in the house, and again recently.
Even if we are not completely in agreement or entirely satisfied with the minister's announcement I think we must all recognize

that it is a step in the right direction, a step which we hope will be followed by many others shortly.
Farm organizations in eastern Canada often have made suggestions to officials of the Department of Agriculture and I think the minister should, in the near future, implement several recommendations made by those organizations, especially the setting up of a feed grain agency for eastern Canada. Then feed grain could be controlled directly by that agency, which in turn would follow the directives of the boards themselves.
Another thing I would like the minister to consider is the securing of markets for the farm production he wants to increase with the help of that new policy.
In any case, I feel it is my duty to thank the minister for that first step which, I hope, will be followed by others shortly to better protect the farmers and give satisfaction to the parties concerned.

subtopic: POLICY ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING FEED GRAINS IN EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we, in this corner of the house, appreciate to a certain extent the improvement that has just been announced with regard to the feed grain situation. Of course, as those who preceded me have stated, we expected a greater improvement. But, as it is often said, when the child begins to walk, it has to take its first steps, and I consider this statement by the minister as a first step toward the improvement of the feed grain market.
On the other hand I am happy, because by allowing the trucking industry to benefit from a subsidy which had always been kept for public enterprise, the government at least made a small gesture toward remedying the troubles of private enterprise, which has been ill-used in the last few years, so much so that it had to pay taxes that the Canadian National Railways might compete with it. This morning's gesture is somewhat of an act of justice toward the trucking industry, because I am sure that with the competition that industry will be able to offer the railways, our eastern farmers will certainly obtain the needed feed grain at a better price.
As do my colleagues, I wish that the committee on agriculture and colonization would take up the study of the feed grain question as soon as possible, so that we may one day see the creation of a feed grain agency for eastern Canada to enable eastern farmers to deal more freely with western farmers in this respect.
Introduction of Bills
Last year the committee on agriculture and colonization left the feed grain question pendant, so to speak, and was to take up its work as soon as possible during the present session. However, I think that "as soon as possible" has been rather delayed, because we have now almost reached the end of the session without having tackled that famous feed grain issue.
Since the beginning of the session the committee has accomplished some very important work, to my mind, but I think that the question of feed grain is most important and that, in a general way, it is of interest to all farmers in Quebec. Indeed, the committee should have been formed right at the start of this session, and the question considered immediately, so as to enable this autumn the eastern farmers to benefit from this subsidy granted private industry.
This subsidy will enable private industry to prove what it can do, in comparison with public enterprise, because the latter reduced its prices, which is help of primary importance for eastern farmers.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister very sincerely and urge him to take the second step as soon as possible.

PROVISION FOR DEFINING LENGTH OF PARLIAMENTARY SESSIONS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-113, to provide for the length of sessions of parliament.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINING LENGTH OF PARLIAMENTARY SESSIONS
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINING LENGTH OF PARLIAMENTARY SESSIONS
speechtext:
This parliament is one of the few remaining parliaments in the world which fails to foreordain or govern the length of its sessions and much of its own business, and this bill is designed as a first step to correct this situation.
The bill would give everybody who desires to have dealings in or with parliament a better opportunity to plan and perform his parliamentary business. It would give parliament a fixed, mandatory session at the outset and an optional one later in the year. The bill defines for parliament the length of sessions but, Mr. Speaker, it defines for the House of Commons only the length of its sittings. It in no way interferes with the sittings of the other place, which is free to control its own sittings.
There are exceptions in the bill. One is in the case of dissolution and the other is in the

Inquiries of the Ministry case of an urgent emergency of national importance. There is a device in the bill which is of interest, I am sure, to all hon. members because it permits the house to be represented by the Speaker, the Clerk of the house and the Sergeant-at-Arms after the house has concluded sittings. This enables the Senate to go ahead with a bill which it passes without amendment and it can become law. The royal assent procedure can be maintained by this device. There are other interesting features about this bill.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, on the orders of the day on July 15 the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency asked whether I was aware of the fact that next fall's "national housing parade" will be seriously jeopardized if C.M.H.C. does not change its lending policy concerning builders.

poration is prepared to make available special assistance in the form of direct loans to permit the construction of display houses. Mr. Speaker, yesterday I undertook to obtain for the house a report on the relationship between certain private litigation in which Harold C. Banks is involved and the appeal of his conviction for maiming Captain Walsh.
My information is to the effect that the present attempt to take Banks into custody arises out of private litigation under the civil law of Quebec between Upper Lakes Shipping Company and Banks. I am informed that the company some time ago obtained an injunction against the S.I.U. and certain officers thereof, including Banks, to prevent them from picketing the company's boats. Some time thereafter the S.I.U. was alleged to have picketed a boat at Three Rivers and the company presented a petition against Banks to the superior court of Quebec. The court adjudged Banks in contempt on account of the picketing and imposed a penalty of 30 days or a month in jail. Now the company is trying to enforce the order of imprisonment.
The federal government has nothing to do with that particular case, and the case in turn has nothing to do with Banks' bail in connection with his appeal from conviction for conspiracy to wound, maim or disfigure Captain Walsh. No condition was attached to the effect that Banks remain in Canada. I would emphasize that it was the considered judgment of the chief justice of the province of Quebec that the most effective means of securing Banks' appearance at the appeal was by means of the bail bond deposited.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I know very well you had no intention-this idea never came to my mind-to impose silence on any member. On the contrary, I think you are to be congratulated for your broadmindedness in that regard.
I was saying that Bill No. C-110 is indicative of a state of mind which exists at the present time in Canada. In this bill we see an encroachment of the federal government in a field reserved to the provinces, that of education. Nine provinces agree to take advantage of this bill, but one province refuses and will act alone in this field.
This is not the first piece of legislation introduced this year and which brings such results. There was the pension plan suggested by the federal government: nine provinces will join this plan and one will not.
The same is true of the bill introduced three weeks ago, concerning the $10 allowance to students aged 16 and 17 years. Nine provinces will join in this plan and one will not.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that more and more such bills will be introduced in the House of Commons and that, more and more, the federal government will try to control all the jurisdiction possible in the nine English speaking provinces, so that, more and more, the nine provincial governments will have nothing to do and we may see their consolidation in the hands of the Ottawa government, whereas, at the same time, the province of Quebec will withdraw from all those joint plans and will administer its affairs by herself. So, before long we shall have only two governments in Canada: the Ottawa government, for the nine English speaking provinces, and the Quebec government for the province of Quebec.
We will then achieve what I forecast yesterday: two governments only, two states, not separated but associated.
Mr. Speaker, I hope this development comes about fairly quickly, more quickly than separatism can progress in Quebec or in any other province, because that is how we will


be able to save confederation, not as it exists at present, with provincial governments, but a new confederation composed of two associated states.
I think the government of the day is in favour of such a development, because it has presented a number of bills along that line. Bill No. C-110 is the fourth one in the course of this one session.
We see the federal government interfering in fields of provincial jurisdiction and nine provinces surrendering their powers to Ottawa while Quebec withdraws from all such programs, having decided it should be the one to look after matters which come under its jurisdiction.
We see Ottawa intruding in the educational field.
It is the tenth measure. The other day, the Minister of Finance said there were nine. With Bill No. C-110, it is the tenth piece of legislation of this type.
The federal government intrudes in the educational field, something to which the provincial government has always objected. The federal government interfered in the field of health, and the Quebec government withdraws more and more from joint plans in this field. The federal government interferes also with regard to highways and the work reserved to the provinces in this connection.
In such a case, we might as well have the same legislation for all. If that is what they want, we have nothing against it. If the other provinces want it, we cannot object to it.
In the field of joint plans, the same thing happens, a single pension plan for the nine provinces and a single pension plan for Quebec. And so on.
In my opinion, it is good to point out the new tendency which now exists in Canada. It is the tendency to have not ten governments but two. The government in Ottawa on one side and the government in Quebec on the other.
That will make up or will enable us to create two states. The state of Ottawa with nine provinces and the state of Quebec with the province of Quebec.
Let us hope that this development will not take too long, so that a new constitution can be drawn up in the light of that new trend, of that new development and that while witnessing that development, Quebec can obtain as soon as possible its autonomy in the fields where it is proud and jealous of its rights, such as education, health, pensions, roads, natural resources, and many others, and that at the same time, Ottawa

will continue-since the provinces want it, since there are nine English speaking provinces that want it and that ask Ottawa for it-to try to achieve as rapidly as possible the union of the nine provinces into one government so that this union of the nine provinces into one government will enable that government and a strong Quebec government to negotiate the terms of a new constitution which will meet the needs of the time, that is in two, three or four years, a constitution tending to settle the problems which could come up between two associate states, the Ottawa state and the Quebec state.
After a thorough examination of all the provisions of Bill No. C-110, I realize that they show a tendency which is nothing new. It has been in existence in Canada for some years. We are heading more and more towards the achievement of that tendency. It is said that, even in Bill No. C-110, the federal government in Ottawa will establish the legal capacity of minors. Then, the federal government will impose regulations to private institutions, that is educational institutions.
Let us recall the words of the Minister of Finance a few days ago, when he said: after all, the majority has some rights in our country.
It is true that the majority has rights in our country, but since when would the majority have the right to bypass the constitution? Of course, if the majority principle was accepted, the majority might impose anything on the minority, and the latter would not be protected by the statutes, the constitution and confederation. Now, the majority has rights, and the fact must be recognized; but the majority in Canada could get its full wishes and rights by setting up a single government for the nine other provinces and a single one for the state of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I think that this trend is not so bad after all. Then, we will arrive at the natural conclusion of what Canada should be, namely the union of two associate states. I do not say two separate states, mind you, but two associate states. Associate means that they co-operate and work together.
I have just been told that if there were only Liberal members in the house at this moment we would not have a quorum. In fact, out of 128 members, there are only five sitting at this time-no, four. I see that there are more than five now, there are six persons, including a member of the New Democratic party who has gone to the Liberal side. There are more on our side, although we are only 13 members. Look, there is 20220-376J

The 1867 act recognized the existence of the two races and granted each province joint powers. Section 91 of the constitution limited the powers of the federal government, while section 92 limited those of the provincial governments. In the list of powers, reference is made to education. That confirms one thing: the evolution of history is following its normal course and today, through Bill No. C-110 and others which have been passed since the beginning of the present session, an attempt is made to give Ottawa various powers which were reserved to the provinces in 1867. In that historical tendency, the rights of Quebec are just the same recognized and I admit it is recognized that it could not participate in such legislation. It is recognized that the province of Quebec has the right to walk or to act alone, independently of the nine other provinces.
Under such circumstances, I think that Bill No. C-110 marks a complete historic evolution which has been going on in Canada for 100 or 125 years. If we vote against Bill No. C-110, it is not that we do not approve of the historic trend, but simply because Bill No. C-110 does not go far enough in that sense. If we vote against Bill No. C-110, it is because we are not at all satisfied with clause 12. Instead of providing for alternative payments, we ask that Ottawa give back to the province its sources of income equivalent to the expenditures incurred under the bill, so that Quebec could itself participate in all the activities of its jurisdiction in the field of education, so that it could levy taxes and take decisions concerning the spending of those taxes.
It is for that reason-because we believe that Bill No. C-110 does not go far enough, besides the fact that Quebec can opt out of the scheme-because that program does not give the province of Quebec its own sources of income to carry out its own scheme of loans and scholarships to students that we are against this legislation.
And so, we will let Bill No. C-110 pass for the nine other provinces, and we opt out of this scheme; but we will object because it does not recognize that the province of Quebec has the right to levy its own taxes and to make its own expenditures in the field of education.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not speak on the bill previously, and as it is a very important bill, not for what it does but for what it does not do, I should like to say a few words.

This is a cheap and very inadequate way in which the Liberal party is honouring an election promise to give education to many people who are now unable to get it. In particular, it is supposed to meet the promise to parents that if the Liberal party were elected there would be scholarships and bursaries for all who need them regardless of which province they are resident in. The Liberal party did not honour this promise of the last election but has come up with a substitute in the form of this bill which will cost the Canadian government approximately $2 million.
Education, Mr. Speaker, as everyone has said, is a very important matter. It is not a field in which we should decide whether a 17 or 18 year old will be able legally to contract a loan which will provide him with an education. We all agree that education should be provided to everyone with the capability of taking advantage of it. That does not mean this assistance should be limited in view of the civil code provisions applying to minors, and matters of bank exchange and other problems which apply in certain provinces although this is the excuse, 1 know.
I think this bill has made two things clear. First of all, the people now know that what the Liberal party promises is not necessarily what it will do. The people who know this are the most important people in the country, the young people who are going to be the leaders of tomorrow as soon as they have completed their education. Second, they will well remember that their education was not granted to them as of right, but that they were allowed to complete their education by a miserable government which lent them money to complete their education, money which should be provided by the nation.
If a person has a college education, taxes will flow into the country, because such people will probably earn three or four times what they would have earned without that education. Therefore in giving to our young people loans of this nature we are not really giving them anything; the $2 million is a very inconsequential figure. If we were to give them $6,000 or $7,000 each to complete their education we would still not be giving them anything.
You will well remember, Mr. Speaker, from personal experience the difference between the income tax you paid when you were earning $8,000 and what you are now paying on your salary, which I think is about equivalent to that of an engineer or others who have had university training. That education has
Loans to Students
raised their standard of living and earning power to that extent. Therefore we are not really giving these students anything; all we are demonstrating is that we in this country have not realized that education is essential. It is still only for the few who can take advantage of it because of the arrangements these people will be able to make.
The $1,000 which we are going to give to a student each year will not put him through university; a great deal more will be required from other sources. For example, the student will have to work part time, or his parents will have to kick through with as much as they had to pay some 10 years ago. As the cost of education grows, so the family will be called upon to put out as much as they did 10 years ago.
This bill has also finally convinced me that the government is not interested in federal aid to education. By passing this bill we have paid no attention to the fact that we in this country should have a national standard of education. It seems to me that if we are going to have a nation, then across that nation there should be a standard of education which each province is prepared to meet. A person going from one province to another should not be put at a disadvantage because of the difference in educational standards which now exist at the university level.
A few years ago, in discussing some of the programs of the military colleges supported by the federal government, we learned that there was one college in one province which had very few graduates from that province, for the simple reason that the educational standards had not been sufficient to enable recruits to meet the entrance requirements; and even when they were given an extra year at military college they were still not up to the academic standing of those in the rest of the provinces. I may say that this province was not Quebec, which we hear has many problems in the field of education.
I think we should face the fact that as far as Quebec is concerned, it already has better legislation than this. Loans to students in the province of Quebec, I am told, are much more attractive than the legislation we are enacting. We are providing this type of credit arrangement in many fields; for example, farm credit, national housing, under the Veterans Land Act, home improvement, farm improvement, fisheries improvement, subsidies to agriculture and mines. We are providing these subsidies on a national basis in many fields, and I wonder why, when we

I do not know whether there is any farm loan scheme in the province of Prince Edward Island-I presume there is-but if not I do not think the reason is that the province might not take advantage of it. Why should we scrap a whole scheme because of the inability of one part of the country to take advantage of it?
The same goes for all the other credit arrangements we have made.
We have not asked that everybody participate equally in them; we are not asking this in education. But I think the government caters to the province of Quebec and allows the tail to wag the dog when it allows the province of Quebec and the representatives of Quebec to decide what the rest of the country is going to have.

I respect those who represent the province of Quebec, but in my opinion they have a wrong impression of what should be accomplished in higher education and the way this program should be financed and arranged. I think we had better face that problem, and if they want to do things this way we should have a meeting and make an arrangement and decide how they want to act. If they

We should quit playing around with this kind of legislation. This Liberal government will have us in a position where we cannot possibly make an arrangement and arrange legislation for the other provinces of Canada that is half satisfactory to those provinces. If we dilute the national course of Canada which most of the other nine provinces want, because of the objection of one province, we are not going to satisfy that province or the other nine provinces either.

Our responsibility is to assist those who will venture in that area, and in addition to provide facilities, air strips and roads, so far as we can economically see the return on that investment of social capital, and it is our responsibility to do these things as rapidly as we can.
I want to say a word now about our parks. Apart from everything else, our national

Supply-Northern Affairs parks are of tremendous importance as a money gatherer and as a considerable factor in the improvement in our balance of our international payments at the present time. I am certain that a great deal of the improvement in recent years in our balance of international payments can be attributed to the attraction of our national parks. I am very proud of them, as I think Canadians generally are. We have recently reiterated our determination to maintain a parks policy which will not permit the exploitation of minerals or forests within them. We think there are sufficient areas in Canada in which exploitation of resources can be carried out without impairing the wilderness aspect of our parks, and that policy will remain.
Last year there were 22 per cent more visitors to our parks than a year ago. Indeed, we are confronted with a crisis in our parks as a result, inasmuch as there has been a complete revolution in the type of person visiting them. Formerly visitors came by train and were relatively wealthy people. Now they are arriving in a veritable torrent of cars on the highways. With a buoyant economy and a prosperous state of affairs generally at the present time, and with the advent of statutory holidays with pay, the average Canadian working man who had not seen the national parks before has put his family into the car and headed for a vacation in a national park; and I think this committee will agree this is one of the finest things that could happen. These people are wanting a type of accommodation different from that which was supplied in the past, and it is difficult for us to keep up with the demand.
I am going to tell the committee frankly that we are being clobbered in some of the parks, though we are moving as fast as we can. People come in and say "Where do I leave the trailer?" or "Where do I pitch the tent?" Many of them have put a large portion of the holiday money into the gas tank and want to spend what is left as economically as possible.
Good highways are, of course, one of the most important reasons for the tremendous increase in the number of visitors to our parks, and in particular the excellent state of the trans-Canada highway has been responsible for the present situation. We have also been concerned about relating our national activities with provincial park activities, and I think this is a good thing, too.
I want to conclude this short review by making a statement on resources. I am sure my predecessor must have given some thought


to the importance and consequence of being the minister of national resources. I have often been described as the minister of "natural resources", and I am sure he was, too. But I am minister of national resources and people sometimes ask "What are these national resources? Are they those exclusively within the Yukon and the Northwest Territories which have not reached provincial status, or is there, otherwise, and elsewhere such a thing as national resources?"
I wish to pay tribute to what I consider to have been one of the most important and valuable conferences ever held in Canadian history, the resources for tomorrow conference held in 1961. That conference produced a document which is, I think, one of the best compendiums of knowledge on natural resources which has been produced by any country in the world. I have not read it all yet, but I have read a great deal of it and I wish this book were required reading for every Canadian. I am certain that the exploitation and development of Canadian resources which has taken place since that time can be attributed at least in part to the revelations made in the splendid papers which were produced at that time.
I am sure some Canadians were hopeful that it would develop immediately into a concrete national resource program. That was not the case, and it is not the case today. I want to say this very frankly. These resources are the responsibility of the crown in the right of the provinces, and the provinces are fully aware of their primacy in this field. It is understandable that this should be so, because their revenues derive largely from them. However, it seems to me that if we are to make the best use of our resources we must come to a concept of national resources as well as regional resources.
To this end we have brought together the resource ministers of the provinces and established a secretariat in Montreal. This is moving in the right direction. If Canadians think we are moving too slowly, I would assure them that because of provincial primacy in this field if we were to attempt to move too quickly we could fail. I may say we have found in a number of instances an increasingly encouraging attitude on the part of the provinces; and I speak of the provinces in unison, not of one province alone. I wish to pay tribute in this regard to the work being done on water resources in the three prairie provinces under the present chairmanship of Hon. Mr. Strom of Alberta. Work is being done with respect to those waters which flow1

from the eastern side of the Rockies, are carried across the three prairie provinces and empty finally into Hudson bay.
Of all our national resources, I want to pay particular attention to water. I will say that in the period immediately ahead water will be the second most important resource, next to the soil itself; and with the attention which is being paid to water at the present time in every part of the world as well as on this continent, it seems to me we should become conscious, both within the provinces and as a nation, of the fantastic resource we have available in our water for multi-use purposes. We shall be asking in the next several years for a considerable increase in the amount of money to be made available for these various studies. The work in the prairie provinces is going ahead excellently, but it seems to me we have to think in extremely broad terms looking one or two generations ahead if we are to use these resources safely at the present time having regard to likely future developments not in Canada alone but on this continent.
It seems to me that particularly with regard to waters which flow across provincial boundaries, here is an example of a field in which we must take action as quickly as we can with the concurrence of the provinces concerned. This is only one example of resource development along the lines of a national concept where making the best use of regional resources confers something to the national benefit; and this, I am certain, is necessary if we are to achieve that power of nationhood which most Canadians want and which I know is within our grasp having regard to the multitude of resources we possess.
That is all I intend to say at this stage. I wish to thank hon. members for the good will which has been shown to me fairly fully in my first year in my present position, as well as for the constructive criticism they have advanced from time to time, more of which no doubt we shall hear today. This is a magnificent department of tremendously wide range. I do not know how long it took the former minister to get a grasp of the department; I have not got a grasp of it yet, though I have been working hard on it. I wish to express my appreciation of the contributions made by members not only on this side of the house but on the opposition benches as well. I am sure that as a result the department will be still further improved.

I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Yukon will speak about the microwave systems, that are going down the Mackenzie river to the Mackenzie delta. I do not want to cover everything in detail; I must leave some of the detail for my colleagues. I hope we might have from the minister a word on tourism in the north because, as is the case in other parts of Canada, I believe the tourist industry is going to be one of the great industries north of the 60th parallel. The Canadian wilderness there is the sort of tourist experience for which North Americans and people from other parts of the world are searching. There has been an encouraging increase in this area, and perhaps the minister at a later stage will give us an up to date report on how the increase in tourism in both territories is moving forward.
Resources have no significance at all outside their development by the human element and the provision for the needs of human resources. The minister made brief reference to the educational program but no reference to the welfare program except to indicate that the housing program that was inaugurated some three years ago is moving forward on schedule.
The human resource aspect of northern development had greater consideration by the former administration than did the natural resource problem. Before you can proceed to develop the natural resources in any developing area or nation you must have a trained labour force. This requires education. You must provide for all the amenities which are a part of the heritage to be expected by people living within the body politic of Canada. This is why we encouraged the vote for the Eskimos. They could not move into the main stream of Canadian life unless they had the stature of first class citizens. This is why a good deal of money was poured into educational facilities in the north. The minister has indicated that 80 per cent of northerners now have the opportunity to attend school. This figure has risen from 15 per cent in the year 1957. It is a tremendous program and one in which Canada can take considerable pride.
The hon. member for Northwest Territories, as an official of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, was responsible for a good part of the welfare program in the western Arctic, and I shall leave any comments in this area to his broad knowledge. There is one comment I should like to make with regard to human resources and it has to do with the problems existing be-


tween the Indian population and the Eskimo population north of 60. The programs are administered by separate departments. There is a lack of uniformity.
I have long been one of those who have supported the viewpoint of Senator Gladstone, the first Indian to sit in parliament, who strongly believes that administrative responsibility for Indians and Eskimos should be brought under the one jurisdiction and should emphasize in no uncertain terms the community development concept. Otherwise we are going to have the same problem that paternalism always brings and which has created such extreme difficulties in our treatment of the Indian population in most parts of Canada over the years. These people must be brought into the main stream of Canadian life on a uniform basis, and by taking into consideration the fact that they can only do so as they move forward as a community.
I know that the department has ambitious plans in this respect. For example, we appointed a director of adult education. It is one thing to educate the youngsters, but in educating the youngsters you are only intensifying the problems of social disorganization because you are educating the children away from the parents. This has been one of the great difficulties in the rapid expansion of educational facilities in the north involving as it does the necessity of transporting these children from their homes to hostel type schools. We were encouraging a local, small family type of hostel unit and I trust this policy is continuing. Otherwise you are going to get a conflict between generations. The children will be educated away from their parents, and this is one of the greatest sources of social confusion and disorganization in any rapidly changing society.
I should like to refer briefly to the Eskimo co-operatives which have been a tremendous success in the north. My last visit to the north in March of 1963 was to attend the first Eskimo co-operative conference at Frobisher. I know that when any minister has responsibility for an important policy of this kind it takes a long time to become fully aware of all its implications. I must say my eyes were opened when I saw these Eskimos from all parts of the Arctic meeting together and discussing their problems in a intelligent and responsible manner.
There was the usual language problem that we have in Canada. The Eskimo dialect of the western Arctic does not correspond to the dialect of the eastern Arctic and the

words of the representatives of the one area had to be interpreted to the representatives of the other area and vice versa. There was also an old Norwegian there whose English was so bad that he had to be interpreted into English. Notwithstanding these difficulties the conference was an overwhelming success.
One of the features of northern development has been the world wide acceptance of the excellent primitive art of the Eskimos. I think one of the most successful good will tours ever carried out on behalf of Canada was that undertaken by Miss Mary Pana-gashoo from Pond Inlet, the editor of the Eskimo magazine, who travelled in several countries in Africa with an exhibit of Canadian Eskimo art. I think that created more good will for Canada than many of the conferences that have taken place at a high political level. It was interesting to note the comment of Miss Panagashoo when she returned. The people who were most interested and most excited about her visit were not necessarily the natives of these countries but rather the Canadians serving in the various embassies. They had never seen a Canadian Eskimo, which indicates just how recently Canada's interest in northern development has emerged.
In recent months Canadian Eskimo art has been replaced in the headlines by Ookpik, the strange little animal that has come to the fore and seems to be becoming the symbol for northern development. I should like to ask some questions concerning Ookpik. Because the Eskimo co-operatives could not supply the quantities demanded, its manufacture has been turned over to commercial interests. This is one thing that we endeavoured to avoid, because the commercialization of Eskimo art in any form results in saturation and a tendency to devalue this art in terms of its monetary return. I hope this point has not been forgotten with respect to Ookpik. Perhaps it would have been better to keep this Arctic animal, the creation of an Eskimo lady at Fort Chimo, in short supply in order to maintain interest because once it gets into the five and ten cent stores and the commercial souvenir market I am afraid it will very rapidly reach the saturation point. I hope that the policy laid down in this respect has not been forgotten by the present administration.
If I may move from the north to parks, everyone is an expert on parks and everyone is interested in parks. We will be hearing from various members on this subject I am sure. I should like to re-emphasize the points
Supply-Northern Affairs that we endeavoured to make when we had administrative responsibility. Recreation and tourism in an age of leisure have precipitated a crisis in our national parks system and to meet the crisis we have got to move a lot faster than we are going at the present time. I hope the minister will expand on what is taking place in the national parks area at this time. There seems to be retrenchment instead of expansion with regard to the policies that were going forward under the former administration. I refer to the establishment of the planning section, the production of reports such as the Oberlander report, park reorganization, the zoning policy laid down in January of 1963 to preserve heavily populated parks such as Banff, Jasper, Waskesiu and Riding Mountain from the damage that will be created if no zoning controls are implemented in these park areas.
Then, there is the policy on recreational parks that we have discussed in this house from time to time. This was to be the next major step forward in the former government's program to meet the rising demand for recreational needs. The camp grounds and picnic grounds program is pretty well completed. The vote indicates it is a rapidly waning program. This has to be met by a broader, more expansive program, namely the recreational parks program whereby the federal government, on the basis of co-operative federalism, will co-operate with provincial governments to provide the recreational parks that are needed in every major urban centre of Canada and which must be provided on a crash program basis if national parks are going to be preserved for future generations which, of course, is their fundamental purpose. We can perhaps discuss this matter at another point in the proceedings.
Historic sites come under parks. There was no mention in the minister's statement as to what is taking place in connection with historic sites. Our program was tied to preparation for the Canadian centennial in 1967. We had launched a program that would have established a major historic site in every province in Canada. Louisburg was the large one, of course, and it received a lot of attention. However, right from Newfoundland, Signal Hill, through to the subArctic regions and the old city of Dawson, the former government had gone ahead in anticipation of the thousands of people who will be coming to Canada in 1967 to present a picture of Canada's historic past that would appeal to the millions of visitors coming to the country. I wonder just how that program

Supply-Northern Affairs is proceeding. There was an idea for animating the historic sites, as has been done with Upper Canada Village and Old Fort Henry. Not only would we have static displays of Canadian history, but we would actually have the historic site presented in animated form which, of course, considerably enhances its appeal to Canadians and the touring public.
I wonder, for example, what are the future plans for the preservation of Dawson city which was rapidly sinking into the permafrost. The whole community had been declared a historic site. While there was criticism from the Liberal party during the period when we had responsibility, I think it was short sighted and I believe it was politically motivated because there were not too many votes involved in the Yukon Territory. The population is small. It was possible to downgrade and ridicule the significance of this historic development because there was not too much political risk involved. This is not the attitude that is required if we are going to maintain a national perspective in the recording and preserving of our historic sites.
I refer on the other hand to the huge expenditures that are going into Expo '67. This will represent an investment of some $165 million, and everybody in Canada heartily approves. Why do they approve? They approve because this is going to be the focal point of our centennial celebration, even though it does involve a deficit of $47 million that will have to be picked up by the federal government. Surely, we are not going to concentrate on one part of Canada, because these millions of visitors will be travelling from Newfoundland right through to the farthest recesses of the north. If we are going to have all our historic attractions, all our recreational attractions prepared for that time, we will have to move a lot faster than we have since the new administration took over.
We talk about the billion dollars that will accrue from tourist spending; we talk about what this will mean in terms of the Canadian economy. The same thing is happening with regard to the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories. We talk about a deficit of half a million dollars, but we do not talk about the increase of $3 million in tourist revenues that resulted from improved tourist business.

I did not want to trespass, and I thank the committee for its courtesy. We must continue the initiative that has been generated by the resources for tomorrow conference. I agree with the minister that this is no easy task because the minister of national resources must assist in providing a program or policy for resources which are substantially owned by the provinces of Canada. I think, Mr. Chairman, you will appreciate just how delicate a matter this is when you consider that at the time we were preparing the resources for tomorrow conference the representative for Quebec was Hon. Rene Levesque who has had something to say about provincial rights and jurisdictions during recent months.
Co-ordination and co-operation are the chief ingredients of success in the field of national policy for resource development. The minister mentioned some of the good things that have already come out of the conference. These are, the national parks association, a voluntary group of citizens that will assist in encouraging public opinion in the support of the fundamental purpose of our national parks system; the federal-provincial parks

conference, which I hope is coming to grips with the recreational parks program that has now been delayed some two years; the ARDA program; the national wildlife federation, which now spans Canada from sea to sea. These are some of the things that have come about already.
The federal government must co-ordinate its activities on resource development. There must be established a council within the cabinet which will bring together the various departments that have joint responsibility in this area. Of course the same must apply to the provinces, but already some of the provinces have managed to co-ordinate their activities. As yet there is no such co-ordination within the government of Canada.
I shall not deal at length with the crisis in water. We had a full scale debate on this matter as recently as last May, and I may say I was amazed at some of the press reaction to that debate, which was a ho-hum reaction-"Isn't there anything more exciting than water to debate?" I think it was a spokesman for the Ralliement Creditiste who referred to the subject as an insipid and colourless one, and the leading editorial in the Ottawa Citizen for May 6 said this:
It was silly of the Conservative opposition to base a want of confidence motion in large part on the great lakes water levels problem-
But as a result of that debate we have become aware that North America, including Canada, is facing a crisis in its water supply, even though we have a large part of the world's fresh water supply within our boundaries. Two conferences have been called on the subject, one by the government of Ontario and the other by the port authority in Montreal. I heartily endorse the minister's remarks when he says we must move forward in the spirit of the resources for tomorrow conference in order to come to grips with the problem as soon as possible. Other hon. members will be talking about power. The export policy that was approved by the former Conservative government has now been approved by this administration. The Columbia treaty project has been approved by this administration. The long distance transmission projects have all been embraced with enthusiasm by this administration and I congraulate it in this regard.
The problem of migratory water fowl has become increasingly difficult in recent years and an international joint committee was established to deal with the matter. Programs of wet land preservation are being carried out, and in my own constituency there is a
Supply-Northern Affairs long lease project extending over a 20 year period that will preserve wet lands for the purpose of the generation of ducks. I would appreciate it if the minister could bring us up to date on how this program is proceeding. Funds must be derived for it. Some consideration was given to the possibility of establishing a duck stamp tax in Canada which would meet the costs of a wet lands preservation program, and I ask whether any progress has been made in this area?
Enough has been said already to establish that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is a most challenging, important and vital department concerned with the interests of Canada's future. The minister has indicated that he accepts the program that was laid down by the former administration. I hope he is successful in persuading some of the doubting Thomases in his own administration to maintain the vigorous pace and pattern of development that took place over the past six years. In particular, with reference to northern administration I hope he will decentralize administrative control into the territories as quickly as it can possibly be accomplished. This is the only way that the north is really going to become a vital part of the Canadian body politic.

It would also have to work out the various fiscal arrangements which would allow the government of Canada to take its rightful position with respect to natural resources. It is true that natural resources are the responsibility of the provinces, yet there are over-all considerations which involve every Canadian citizen, and it is with this aspect of course that the minister is most concerned. I think it would be of assistance to him if there were some permanent office to co-ordinate the various efforts made by the provinces and the federal government.
In British Columbia, national resource conferences are held and they have proved very productive. I know that the minister, who comes from British Columbia, is very familiar with the work which has been done by these conferences over the years. Water is, of course, one of the greatest resources of the world and we are especially favoured in Canada in this respect. When the early settlers came to Canada they used the rivers and lakes for the purpose of transportation. As other methods of transportation were found they became interested in water more

from a standpoint of its capacity to generate power. Now we are talking about the multiple use of water, and indeed we are returning to the use of water as an aid to transportation. In this connection I refer to the float plane. I believe a great deal of imagination will have to be used in order to develop a policy which will be of assistance in many places where float plane travel is increasing, and I should like to enlist the assistance of the minister in dealing with his colleague the Minister of Transport in this connection, because I believe the hon. gentleman could exert a considerable influence on the Department of Transport. As he knows, most of the work now being done in the northern regions is made possible through the use of these float planes, and there is a great deal which the Department of Transport could do in conjunction with the department of northern affairs to facilitate the employment of small aircraft in these areas.
Some members of this committee are alarmed at the possibility of power developments taking place at the expense of the salmon fishery. This is particularly true with regard to the proposed construction on the Fraser river. I should like to point out however, since the particular construction proposed on this river lies within my constituency, that there are very few salmon spawning grounds which will be affected; an insignificant amount of salmon spawning would be affected by the establishment of a water reservoir on the north fork of the Fraser or on the McGregor river. This is one of the streams which at certain times in the spring, if it happens to unload its belch of water coinciding with flooding in the lower Fraser valley, has been shown to be an important factor in connection with Fraser valley flooding. I do not think we need to be too concerned in that regard.
As far as recreation and wildlife is concerned, let me remind hon. members that the addition of water surfaces that would follow the damming of these streams would provide a great deal of opportunity for recreation and for use by the float planes we were talking about a while ago. And of course sportsmen could use them for fishing and recreation.
We are interested in our section of the country in this question of providing additional water for the prairies. Evidence was given in the external affairs committee when the Columbia river was under study that water from the Peace river, after it had been used as a source of power, could be diverted successfully to the prairie region. This is one
Supply-Northern Affairs of the studies which needs to be pursued with a view to obtaining water for the prairies from the area which I represent. I think it is a logical step and I think it is one which will provide both irrigation and power to the people of south Saskatchewan. In this connection the use of water for irrigation is often overlooked by the people concerned. They tend to think more in terms of power generation. This is a short range view, though I agree the generation of power is an important part of these developments.
As members know, I come from an area which is recognized as the white spruce capital of the world. We ship enough lumber out of Prince George alone in one year to build a city almost the size of Edmonton; a trainload of lumber leaves there seven days a week, 365 days a year.
This puts one in the position where we must recognize the tremendous value of the forests of Canada. The forests are the natural resources of the provinces, and here again we have an over-all Canadian interest. But I think much more could and should be done. This is where we overlap once more with the Department of Forestry. Therefore we must hope that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will get together with the Minister of Forestry and see whether a much more liberal and broad scheme cannot be worked out to pay much more attention to the forests of Canada than has been paid in the past. I think that when the minister was in British Columbia he dealt with this matter, and I want to congratulate him on the interest he has shown in this regard. I am sure the people of Canada generally will appreciate any efforts made to bring about accomplishment along these lines.
As far as our parks are concerned I have one special interest of which the minister is well aware. I was pleased to note in the Western Producer an article which said that the minister has stated, as he has said to me privately, that when the British Columbia government gets the road from the western boundary of the Jasper national park completed, he will construct a highway from the town of Jasper to that boundary, a distance I believe of some 19 miles. However, I would warn the minister that once "flying Phil" gets moving on that proposition he will be speeding right along, and perhaps he should keep that in mind.
1 hope I am not wrong about this, but I would predict, knowing the good intentions of the minister, that a good highway will be constructed from the western boundary

Supply-Northern Affairs "through to Kamloops, and opened to traffic, before the minister completes construction of his road from the town of Jasper to the western boundary. I do not say this because I think the minister will fall down on his job; I just think that the circumstances will be such as to make it most difficult to be able to get this construction completed in the short time available to him. I do not anticipate that it will be very long before the road I speak of, highway No. 5, will be completed.
