I am told that the red tape in such cases is even worse than entering the United States.
I do not believe we should have this sort of foreign land in Canada. The railway companies have a right of way through the parks, and I think the highways system should provide for people not interested in the park itself but merely travelling from point A to point B a right of way. These people should not be put in the position of being stopped and checked, and all the rest of it, on entering a park.


Some of the experiences of the people in McBride and Valemount with regard to moving equipment from Edmonton have been rather disturbing, and the situation there has been a continual source of irritation. Once we get the traffic we would expect and have been experiencing in the Rogers pass, and which we may expect when the highway to Prince Rupert through Kamloops and Yel-lowhead is completed, the flow will be so heavy that in my view it will be nonsensical to let the situation in our parks remain as it is today with regard to people wanting to travel through the parks.
I should like to deal very shortly with the question of the Alaska highway. Here we come to a situation where the department involved is not the Department of Forestry but the Department of Public Works. I know that the minister has on various occasions shown a keen interest in this matter, and I think we agree wholeheartedly on what should be done. However, there are certain obstacles of which the minister is aware. I should like to put on record what I think should be our procedure in connection with the Alaska highway.
This is a road leading to northern resources, and it is a very important road. I think the highway should be built by Canada and by Canadians. I do not believe that we should enter into contracts or negotiations with the United States which would allow the United States actually to participate in the building of the highway. I say that because the value of labour and machinery to the people in the United States compared to the people in Canada is so vastly different that we could run into a great deal of difficulty, which I think should be avoided.
Those parts of the Alaska highway which lie within the known alignment of the final survey of the highway under the reconstruction program should be paved as soon as possible. I do not think that we should wait in this regard for any negotiations with the United States. The minister has received a letter from the minister of highways in British Columbia saying that that government would share the cost on a 50-50 basis of paving the road to the northern border of British Columbia.
I think the federal government should take British Columbia up on this offer. Having done so, negotiations could be carried on with the United States as to what is their responsibility in connection with the Alaska highway. Having decided upon that responsibility in due course, we in Canada would be in a posi-

tion to accept a cheque from the United States with regard to their responsibility. It as a result of these negotiations there is to be reimbursement to the province of British Columbia, because it would then become a three-way split instead of a two-way split with regard to the area from mile 83 to the border, British Columbia could be paid for that portion in view of the change.
I think these are important suggestions, Mr. Chairman, because we all know that in dry weather-and there is a lot of dry weather in that country-a large truck can be travelling on the Alaska highway for miles and miles and miles and the driver will never know whether there is anybody behind him, so that the people behind the truck can never get by. This leads people to commit suicide, in that they get so fed up with the dust and dirt that they are prepared to take a chance on passing the truck. Sometimes it is their last chance.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Does this happen right in your own riding?

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Yes, this is right in my own constituency. I am not very far from home when I am talking about the Alaska highway. I think this type of hazard is something that should be eliminated as quickly as possible. Even a mile or two of paving here and there would allow a truck driver to see, on those stretches of highway, whether there was a line-up of cars behind him, and he could let them get by. It would also alert him to the fact, as he is more or less daydreaming along the highway at 35 or 40 miles an hour, that there are people behind him and it would give him a chance to look out for some place where he could let them get by. I recall very, very vividly a situation where I passed through the town of Golden, and shortly after passing through the town on the Big Bend highway I came behind a truck. The only time I was able to get by this truck was when we passed over the bridge at the Canoe river. For almost 100 miles we were behind the truck and we could not get by. When the truck driver got on to the bridge, he noticed the line-up of cars he had bottled up behind him, and I was one of them. This is the sort of thing that happens on the Alaska highway. I would hope that if these barriers still exist, they can be broken down so that work on this project can be commenced immediately.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to commence my comments on the minister's estimates by adding my endorsation of the
Supply-Northern Affairs praise which he extended to his officials. Both assistant deputy ministers sitting in front of the minister are fairly new to the respective positions they now hold, although Mr. Cot6 was, of course, an assistant deputy on the parks side for some years before assuming his role as deputy minister of the department. I think Mr. Gordon, the assistant deputy minister replacing Mr. Cunningham- and all of us regret Mr. Cunningham's death soon after he left the department-will do an outstanding job, having regard to his past record in the service of Canada. I should not stop there, Mr. Chairman, because the same praise should be extended throughout the department of the minister. I am familiar with many of the personnel in the department, and in all my dealings with them I have found them to be most co-operative, most dedicated and most hard-working in so far as the good of the north and the carrying out of the various responsibilities under their charge are concerned.
I have on several occasions come to my feet in the house and directed questions to several ministers-the Minister of Labour, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and others

with respect to consultation with the people both in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories with regard to federally conceived and federally sponsored schemes which affect the lives and the welfare of northerners. I believe that a major step forward in accomplishing the desires of the people of the north was taken yesterday when the government accepted the principle-of consultation in the student loans legislation which the Minister of Finance had before the house. This is the beginning. I suggested' to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who was in his seat at that time, that there should be the creation of' some permanency about this consultation, because while we may be blessed in the future with benevolent and enlightened ministers of northern affairs, and deputies,, assistant deputies and commissioners, it is undesirable in my view, and in the view of many I am sure, that there should be an assumption by the administration that it is expressing the views of people who live in the north.
One of our main complaints, regardless of which government was in power at the-time, has been that we suffer from the fact that we are 4,000 miles away from the seat of administrative direction here in Ottawa..
5952	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs Many of those who have responsibility for making decisions affecting the future of the people who live in the north have never been there, or if they have been there it has only been for one, two or three days. In this sense we feel we are being governed by remote control. I am sure this complaint has been heard often by the deputy minister, who has been associated with the department for a number of years, and it was heard often by his predecessor. I am sure the minister himself, during his travels through the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, brief though they were, heard the same sort of comment with respect to the people in that part of the country being heard. It is not a new complaint. Indeed, I have in my hand what might be called the initial issue of the Yellowknife Blade, which was published in 1946. It is dated March 14, 1946, and here is the substance of it:
A meeting sponsored by the Northwest Territories association will be held in the community hall on Friday, March 15, at 8 p.m., to protest the actions of the administration; to demand the application of the principle of democracy in our government. We are free men in a free country. Let our voice be heard! God save the King!
This is still the feeling in the north.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: It is the feeling in Vancouver city, too.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
It may be the feeling in Vancouver but I am sure the minister appreciates the depth to which this feeling goes in the north where there is direct responsibility and direct administration by the government here in Ottawa. Most of our activities in the Yukon revolve around decisions of the federal government because natural resources, a sphere in which the federal government is most active in the north, are a direct responsibility of the federal government. The commissioner who is directly responsible for the administration of the affairs of the Yukon, and the same is true in the Northwest Territories, is directly responsible to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, so that whatever the commissioner does reflects, rightly or wrongly, on the minister's own administration. This has always been the case and will continue to be the case until there is a separation of executive and legislative functions in the governments of the two territories.
I believe that great strides were made, particularly during the years 1957 to 1963, in ameliorating this situation. For the first time since the Yukon became a territory a Yukoner has been appointed commissioner


of the territory. This is a very valuable step not only in ensuring that the department will get closer to the views of the people who live there but also because they will have the benefit of the knowledge of a man who has lived for many years of his life in the territory. I am sure it will be a happy day indeed for the people who live in the Northwest Territories when the same policy is adopted there, although I must say the present commissioner, Mr. Sivertz, has a fund of extremely valuable information which he can apply to the problems that exist in the Northwest Territories.
By the amendment to the Yukon Act in 1960 we embarked on the beginning of the road to self government. I do not know what the minister's personal views may be with respect to following the formula which I put before his predecessor in office, and the one before that with respect to development of responsible government in the Yukon. I feel that the minister, whoever he may be and whichever party is in power, must adopt a policy of gradually increasing the size of the Yukon legislative council as the population increases, not as the tax revenues to the federal treasury increase-although these are substantial now so far as the Yukon is concerned. As the population increases, so should the size of the council itself, following a plan similar to that which existed with regard to the former northwest territories which became the province of Manitoba.
I am sure the minister in his reading has come across the efforts of Mr. F. G. Haultain at that time who led the struggle for the development of responsible government in the northwest territories of that day. It is that type of formula I am thinking of, so that when we reach the stage that we have a council composed of a sufficient number of representatives to allow the formation of a cabinet form of government we can look forward then to the development in the immediate future of a province in the Yukon.
Again, there are many people who believe that he who pays the piper should call the tune. This was not the case with the province of Manitoba. At that time the federal government still bore the major cost of developing educational facilities, roads, other resources and communications. There are responsible businessmen in the Yukon who will come forward to serve on any legislative body when the territory reaches the size that we can look forward to responsible government, and who will be just as capable in administering funds, whether from federal or territorial

sources, as are those, capable though they may be, who now perform this function in the administrative side of the government both in the territory and at Ottawa. The same reasoning can be advanced for passing on this responsibility to the elected representatives of the people in the Yukon as was followed in the case of the schoolboard at Yellowknife which administers a good portion of federal funds. The principle is the same in the two cases.
There is one point where I differ with the minister. His predecessor, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, has said that the minister accepts the northern development program of the former government. I have not seen evidence in the north of this wholehearted acceptance. I look around in the Yukon, for instance, and the only development road I see going ahead right now is the last section of the road from Watson Lake to Boss river.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
They pooh-poohed the
vision of the north.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
All of the engineering is now complete on the road that was approved by the previous administration from Ross river to Carmacks. All the minister now needs to do is to convince his colleagues, as I am sure he has tried to do, to approve construction of that road and the tenders will go out immediately.
While I am on the subject of roads I would ask the minister to detail for the benefit of the committee and for my own benefit the changes in policy which have taken place since the change in administration. I note that there is under consideration now the question of whether or not the government is going to continue to contribute financially to the cost of access road construction in the Yukon. As the minister knows, this was a definite policy of the previous administration. If a mining company had a property which it wanted to develop and which required the construction of a road from an existing communications facility to their property, the federal government would make a financial contribution to the cost of that road. Is that policy being continued? If it is, is it being continued to the same extent as under the previous government? I have some doubts on this score and I should like them to be set at rest because I know of two applications that have been made, one as long ago as 10 months, and the federal authorities have not yet been heard from with respect to whether or not they are going to contribute. I am not
Supply-Northern Affairs going to mention any names but the point is that the applications have been made.
I hope the government will not revert to their pre-1957 policy when the pioneer in the oil exploration industry, Western Minerals, made application for financial assistance in the construction of a winter trail from Flat creek to Eagle plain and were turned down. They did not receive a penny by way of assistance in getting their equipment in to discover the first oil and gas well in the Yukon, which they did in 1959 or 1960. The minister knows that today extensive oil and gas exploration is going on in the Yukon, and the possibilities of combining the exploitation of this resource, which is known to be there, with the huge deposits of iron ore in the Snake river area are beyond comprehension. The combined development of these two resources in this area of Canada will make no small contribution indeed to the over-all fabric of Canada.
I was very happy to hear the minister announce in reply to my question the other night that the C.N.R. is co-operating to the fullest extent with the owner of these mineral claims in the survey of a railroad route, which I presume is going to proceed through the Mayo area into the Snake river area, to assess the feasibility of construction of a railroad to transport the product from its existing location.
Just the other day I read a report by the Peso silver mine, and some very eminent geologists contributed to that report which came into my hands. They estimate that in the Mayo, Keno and Calumet areas there exists almost one billion tons of silver lead ore. The government is extracting from one operating company about half a million dollars a year in corporate taxes, to say nothing of the personal income taxes that come from the 700 or 800 miners who work in the area.
The minister in his travels has said the government intends to place emphasis on private investment in the north. Although I have raised the matter on two or three occasions he has not assured me, and I hope he will during the discussion of his estimates, that by saying that emphasis was going to be placed on private investment in the north, he did not mean the government was pulling in its horns in the encouragement of an operating partnership between the federal government and private enterprise in the development of the north. Let there be no mistake, Mr. Chairman, this project of developing Canada's northland for all Canadians, for national benefit, is a joint project which

Supply-Northern Affairs must be undertaken with the federal government assuming its full responsibility in the way of programs which will encourage the investment of risk capital to develop the resources.
What we said, what the then prime minister said in 1957-58, what the minister of northern affairs, now the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, said, was that we must create an atmosphere by government activity in the creation of communications, in the creation of other facilities, which will attract private investment into the north. As a result of the adoption of these policies, and perhaps as a spillover, we see today what the minister has referred to as private investment in an amount never before experienced in the Yukon. There is perhaps one other year which would have come close to this year so far as mineral exploration and development activities in the Yukon is concerned and that is 1953 when the Hudson Bay Mining Company uncovered vast low grade deposits of nickel ore near Kluane lake.
This is what the then deputy-and I am referring to Mr. Robertson who is now the clerk of the privy council-had to say about this partnership when he spoke to the national northern development conference sponsored by the Edmonton chamber of commerce on Thursday, September 18, 1958 in Edmonton:
In developing the material and human resources of the north we are encouraged, on the one hand, by a new readiness on the part of the public to see government accelerate its efforts and, on the other, by a new awareness on the part of private enterprise of the exciting possibilities of this vast and promising area. Government- at both the federal and provincial levels-is responding, and there is every indication that it will continue, on a steadily increasing basis, to do its part in the process of development under our system. It will be the responsibility of private enterprise to follow through with imagination, drive and efficiency-and with a consciousness of its responsibility in this great initiative.
This teamwork for development is not only a mark of the effective functioning of our system and an earnest of our faith in the future but it can and will be a warranty to all our people that the Canadian north will one day hold a place of honour in our progress as a nation.
Specifically with regard to the government's role in development policies, he said this:
It is clear that government, in its role under our philosophy not only provides the basic services expected of government such as health, education, law and order, and necessary administrative and regulatory services, but in a number of other important ways can do much to provide the basis for the industry and finance that can then carry forward with resource development.


But why should it? It is of some importance -both to government and to private enterprise- to be clear and to keep clear the reasons why, in Canada, we have decided throughout our national history that it is a proper role for government to assist private enterprise in resource development.
Now, I hope that is the policy of the minister. I hope that he is not going to leave resource development in the north to private investment initiative. As I said, it would appear that despite what I conceive to be the feelings of the minister in this regard, and certainly from what I gather from the speeches he has made in various parts of the country, there has been a retarding of the tempo of government attention to resource development in the north. The minister was quoted in Vancouver, speaking before the chamber of commerce there, as referring to a bold, booming vision of the north. In this connection he was speaking specifically of the road from Flat Creek which has now reached Chapman lake and which it was contemplated would traverse the Eagle plain and Peel plateau and go through to Fort McPherson.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I have been careful to avoid the word "vision".

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: I can understand that.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
I commend to the minister the word "vision". It was not right, and I am sure he will agree it was not, nor was it accurate for members of his party when they were sitting on this side of the house to refer to the vision of the north as a nightmare. It was just as inaccurate and improper for the then opposition to have ridiculed and scorned a development program which was conceived, not for the people of the north or for the voters in the north, or because there is only one seat there and one in the Northwest Territories, but because the holders of that vision had the conviction, and still do, that by following a program that was developed within the department as well as within the political caucus it would assist the development of the vast and rich potential of the northern areas for the benefit of all Canadians. I think it is trite to say that these resources belong to the people of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. What Canadians as a whole I think fail to appreciate, even though it was attempted with great force and vigour to bring this home to them in describing the vision of the north in 1957-

58 and in the years since, is that these resources are theirs, too.
This almost 50 per cent of Canada, to which the minister referred in his opening remarks, belongs to all Canadians, and it is in their interests and in the interests of the nation to develop these resources. It is in the interests of the over-all national economy, just as it was in the interests of the national economy that Canadians should build the Canadian Pacific Railway in the early days of our national development. Had that visionary project not proceeded at that time, where would we be? How late would the country be in developing the vast, potential riches of the west? As my hon. friend from the Northwest Territories points out, being a westerner I would probably be a congressman instead of an M.P.
The minister mentioned tourism and highways. He mentioned water as being second only to the soil as a natural resource. I hope he will have something to say during discussion of these estimates as to what the government is doing about the plans of the United States for the construction of the Rampart dam project. I believe this should be viewed with alarm now by the Canadian government, because once the United States decides to proceed with the construction of the Rampart dam project we run squarely up against the provisions of the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act and in all likelihood, if that project proceeded, we would be seriously impeded in developing the full potential of the Yukon river watershed which, as the minister knows, contains twice the existing potential of the St. Lawrence seaway project, a power project that the imagination at the moment cannot even conceive.
Once there has been established a national power grid, which was one of the developmental programs that was being blueprinted by the previous government and which this government has, as has been stated in the house, adopted and intends to carry through, there is no reason why the Yukon river hydroelectric power potential cannot be developed, again for the benefit of all Canadians. I find myself in full agreement with the minister when he places such emphatic importance on the water resources of the country.
The minister also spoke of national parks. I shall not embarrass him by asking what progress is being made with the establishment of a national park in the Yukon. That responsibility, at the time of the change of government, rested with the Yukon legislative 20220-377
Supply-Northern Affairs council and I believe it is still in that stage. You have a complete failure of the two groups in the Yukon to reconcile a meeting of minds on this matter. The mining people say that the establishment of any park will curtail mineral exploration and development. On the other hand you have those who are interested in the aesthetic intentions of the national parks principle, and the two cannot get together. In correspondence and in personal discussion, I have expressed my own view to the minister. I hope the problem will soon be resolved, but if it is to be resolved the initiative rests with the local representatives on the territorial council.
When the minister speaks before chambers of commerce in Vancouver, when he speaks in Dawson Creek of communications, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce speaks of oil and gas policy and the national power grid-all of these involving as they do a national development policy and a northern development policy as part of that national development policy-I cannot help thinking back to speeches such as that made by the former hon. member for Laurier, Mr. Chevrier, who is now the high commissioner in London, when he said in the maritimes that he was sick to his stomach of all this talk of northern development, that money should be spent in the provinces where there were more people and where there was more justification for spending it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: More voters.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
That is it-more voters. Let us face the fact that that is why we received all the criticism we did of the vision of the north. That is why all this criticism was generated over the Dawson city festival. Now we are spending $8 million on landscaping in Montreal, yet the opposition of that day ridiculed, scoffed and sneered at an investment that not only would have saved an ailing city but would have established a permanent economic return from tourism in the Yukon. The same argument that is now being used to justify a $47 million deficit in world fair expenditure was used by us to justify the Dawson city festival, yet when we sat on that side of the chamber we were laughed at for spending some $700,000 of federal moneys to restore the Grand Palace theatre and the steamer Keno at Dawson city.
I hope that the minister sees it as Pierre Berton does, and I think we are all aware of Mr. Berton's political leanings. As reported in a recent press release, when he was in

Supply-Northern Affairs Charlottetown speaking about centennial projects-
-Mr. Berton was asked about tourist developments in Dawson city and what had happened to what was once a "courageous experiment." He answered that "the courageous experiment was ruined by cowards."
And so it was.
He said that two things were done-a theatre was restored and a famous river boat was restored. People "began to scream that too much money was being spent," he said, "and the next year the government pulled the rug out from under that town and now it stands there with an empty monument and an empty steam boat." He cited this experience as an example of "the lack of faith that people have in this country, the lack of enthusiasm, this terrible dead por-ridgey apathy."
I would urge the minister to take a hard second look at the continuation of the Dawson city festival. The plant is now there. The local visitors association has organized a show in the Grand Palace theatre during the tourist season. It is called "The Drunkard", and I imagine the Minister of Transport would have something to say about that, particularly having regard to his descriptions of Arizona Charlie and his caricature in the Globe and Mail as "Pick's purity patrol," where he was depicted as Carrie Nation with a hatchet smashing up the bottles on the shelves in Arizona Charlie's.
This project is worthy of the minister's consideration. His deputy minister, who now sits in front of him, was one of the strongest enthusiasts for the Dawson city festival. I sat in on a meeting with him, and if the minister has any regard for his deputy's views on this matter he will take a hard second look at re-establishment of the festival. There were others in the department who had faith in that project but there were some, I can recall, at certain meetings who, once it looked as though it was going to be a political embarrassment-and it was successfully made a political embarrassment but by those who did not have that faith they should have had in the ultimate success of the project-deserted it like rats in a sinking ship. They denied any paternity for the project, one which was worth while, which produced tourists, and is still doing so.
Tourism in the Yukon, as elsewhere, is one of the most important industries in Canada today, and could be the most important industry in the Yukon in the very near future if mining development does not proceed with that impetus we expect.

I thank the committee for its indulgence.
I have one or two further specific questions to address to the minister. I believe the minister should inform the committee, if he can, precisely what the intentions of the government are with respect to introducing legislation amending the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. Mining companies and the mining industry generally are interested in something more precise than the statement that legislation might be introduced in the fall or next spring, the words the minister used in a personal conversation with me some weeks ago.
I should also like to have a statement from the minister telling us precisely what road projects are in hand for this fall or next summer in the Yukon, and I imagine my hon. friend from the Northwest Territiories would be interested to know what is to be the program in his region as well.
I should like the minister to tell us what has happened to the interdepartmental committee on agricultural development in the north. What progress has that committee made? It made one report at the time the government changed, but that is the only report in existence. 1 have asked about this before. I should also like to know what progress has been made in unsnarling the existing land program in the Yukon. What progress has been made in this regard? What has been done to make it easier for farmers and small holders to obtain property in the Yukon? The last I heard, a farmer who wanted to purchase acreage there had to pay $16 an acre for land, which was certainly not prime land, while land in the Peace river area is selling for around $3 an acre.

I wish also to draw a very important matter to the attention of the minister in the

course of these few concluding remarks. The minister knows that the Yukon legislative council or, to be absolutely correct, the commissioner in council, has exclusive jurisdiction over the expenditure of moneys from the Yukon consolidated revenue fund. A practice exists-I can only call it a practice, because 1 do not think it has the sanction of law- and has existed for a number of years, of allotting a particular portion of Yukon revenue for expenditure by individual councillors. I speak here of the tax of 25 cents per bottle which is levied on liquor in the Yukon, revenue from which is allocated specifically for community development. This would be acceptable if the revenue in question were placed in the territorial consolidated revenue fund, as it should be, and made subject to the authority of the commissioner in council. But what happens is this: These funds are allocated on a per capita basis to the seven councillors who represent the seven ridings in the Yukon, and these councillors have direct authority to say how these moneys are to be spent and in which communities-

Mr. Chairman, every year when the northern affairs estimates come up since I have been a member of parliament for the riding of Bow River I have always had great pleasure in saying a few words, particularly regarding our national parks. In my introductory remarks I should like to say to the minister that as one member of the opposition I appreciated his statement; in fact I told him so in a note. I thank him for the forthright manner in which he dealt with some of the problems not only of the north but of the parks.
I must say at the outset that I, like the minister, have always been one who believes that under proper rules and regulations free enterprise will do more to develop our parks and encourage and serve the tourists than if they are under government control. If I understood the remarks of the minister properly, he followed that line of reasoning today.
As far as some of our park facilities are concerned, with which I will deal in a few moments, I agree with him that there have been some serious developments concerning our tourists. After all, the Banff national park was the first national park in Canada.
If I may take a moment or two, I should like to say that the national park at Banff is the site where the Kootenay and Shuswap Indians, fleeing from their traditional enemies the Blackfoot Indians, both of which are Indian races now and have a reserve in the constituency of Bow River, settled, long before 1800 when David Thompson became the first white man to arrive in the Rockies. However, not until the railway came there in 1881 in search of a route through the mountains did the community grow.
Banff was known, as the minister and no doubt his officials are aware, as Siding 29. Then after 1885 it became the Banff national
Supply-Northern Affairs park. The area of Banff national park is probably almost the size of, if not larger than, Prince Edward Island and is situated in the mountains, extending from the foothills and up into the mountains bordering the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. The early pioneers of Banff did a tremendous job. When one talks about doing a tremendous job he has to be very careful, because there is that school of thinkers who believe that if you develop anything in a park you might disturb something. I am talking of those people who have done something very important and who, on their own initiative and with their own capital, established certain businesses such as motels, restaurants and various other enterprises, in conjunction with the C.P.R., to build up a multimillion dollar industry, the tourist industry. Last year more than 1,000,000 people went through the gates of Banff national park and spent their money there. As the minister has properly said, and as other ministers have said, this helps our imbalance of trade, particularly with respect to United States dollars.
I agree that there has been a greater influx of tourists, and this has been brought about for two reasons. One is the completion of the highway through Rogers pass and the other is the devaluation of the dollar, which was pegged at 92J cents. I am not going to get into a nasty field here, but this pegging of our dollar was very much criticized by the Liberals during the election campaign in 1962, when we got into a minority position. I have always said it was that issue that put us on this side of the house. The minister says that he now sees a tremendous development in the north, and he spoke in glowing terms about the railway development, and so on. He said to me previously- though not in these exact words-that he did not go along with the Prime Minister, who said that the building of the railway to Great Slave lake was utter nonsense, or something like that. I will read his remarks in a few moments. But today we see the minister in a new position because he is a man of responsibility.
I was speaking about the pioneers in this area, Mr. Chairman. There are fellows like William Simpson, who went in there before 1900 and is still there just north of lake Louise. He has an operation there and a tourist attraction in the way of a motel and other facilities. We have people like Cooper and the early people who went to Banff. These people have made a tremendous contribution in this respect, and they have to be protected

Supply-Northern Affairs because the tourist season, as the minister and his parliamentary secretary know, is a very short season. To date it has been a very short season because basically the parks were developed so that people could come and see the beauty of nature, but also because the influx of people is during the months of July and August when families come to visit the parks.
There is now a new atmosphere developing in this respect. The idea now is not only to attract more tourists during the summer but to develop our national parks-Banff and the lake Louise area-as winter sports centres. Someone told me not long ago-and I am sure the parliamentary secretary will be interested in this-that it is a pretty cheap holiday to go from Montreal into the state of New York for skiing, because they have special rates, and so on. If we are to compete at lake Louise in this respect we have to have winter sport facilities. That is the first suggestion I make to the minister. I know it has been opposed by certain people in the department, particularly one person. I will single him out in a few moments. This gentleman does not believe in developing the parks for this sort of thing. However, I still think we could have the winter games and sports facilities in these parks and would not be disturbing the national beauty of our parks.
I read an interesting article in Time magazine of April 14, 1961. George Hees, then minister of transport and later minister of trade and commerce, was out skiing when they opened up the ski road at lake Louise. He said he had skied everywhere in the world-and he was quite a sportsman-and that no snow, conditions, view or beauty exceeded those existing in this area. This is what appeared in Time magazine. This is why I like the minister's new approach; he has endeared himself to me this afternoon, and I am sure he is expressing the views of his parliamentary secretary in this regard when he says the situation has changed. We are not back in the horse and buggy days. I shall read what somebody said in the department. I never could find out who it was, although I have my suspicions. In fact, he is probably listening to me right now:
Staff members of the national parks branch were less agreeable. Said one: "Private interests naturally are always putting pressure on the national parks system. Hees was going along. He is quite uninformed."
At that time I would have liked to get that gentleman on some skis going down Whitehorse mountain, just to see how he would accomplish the feat, after Hees went


down on that occasion when the Olympic champion was there.
We have had to fight this situation for a long time. I am very pleased therefore to hear the minister say there is a new approach in this regard; that the old, narrow interpretation applied to the parks legislation is now being changed; that we should do things in our parks; that the scope was there all the time and it was only the administrators' interpretation of the legislation that held us back. I am pleased to learn of this change. I am also happy to learn that the minister has been able to sell that change and I want to congratulate him on that; because I and others have tried to sell this idea to the people in charge. That is a pretty tight-knit department, if there ever was one. You only have to go to Banff and talk to the people about this and they will confirm that fact. I am only speaking for them here; I am sure if they were here themselves they would be able to do a better job.
Mr. Chairman, before going on with a few suggestions in regard to the parks, I would like to say something with regard to northern affairs. I have here a map of Canada which shows Melville island, Hubert island, and so on, away up to Alert point. I have just been told by the hon. member for Northwest Territories that Alert point is 2,350 miles north of Winnipeg. From my apartment door in Ottawa to my home in Scarborough, Calgary, it is 2,600 miles; so it is almost as far from Winnipeg to Alert point as it is from Ottawa to Calgary. Therefore we appreciate how vast is the north.
One thing has always concerned me since I became a member in 1958 and sat on the committee dealing with northern affairs. I do not say this in a critical way, but it is very important. No one has been able to tell me just where exactly is our northern boundary. We might go to the north pole; but we have some suggestion through the newspapers, through people who have been up in that area, through little leakages from people on the D.E.W. line, and others, that there are little outposts of other countries established on land which we believe to be Canada's. I do not know whether that is true, but if it is I say to the minister that surely there has come a time in the tide of Canadian affairs when this country must have four boundaries delineated. But we do not seem to have a northern boundary; at least, we do not know exactly where it is. We should work this out. If we cannot finance it ourselves, probably with the assistance of the United States and

others concerned with the defence of North America it could be worked out. We should employ oceanographers and other scientific men in this regard to determine where our northern boundary is and push our civilization further forward to make sure that what we now believe we hold will remain Canadian.
I have said that it is 2,400 miles from Alert point to Winnipeg. This is a vast area of our country. We have heard the hon. member for Yukon on several occasions; we have heard the minister and others talk about the vast resources of the north. Those resources are there. Let us make sure they stay Canadian. To do this we should now take a serious look at the matter of establishing our northern boundary. I put this suggestion forward as a constructive suggestion, Mr. Chairman, and not in the way of criticism. We should establish this boundary, because I have always thought that a country had to have four boundaries. I know we have had a lot of boundary disputes and this question has caused a great deal of trouble in the world.
Next, what about the defence of North America? This is very, very important, and is another reason why our northern boundary should be fixed. Of course, the map I have here is a Canadian map and perhaps we might be a little prejudiced; but it shows a red line up at the north pole, and there is another red line half way down. It may be that the Soviet union or some other countries consider that they own some of this land. Therefore, I say it is time to move, to march in this direction and find out where our northern boundary really is. That is why I posed that question to the minister when he was speaking in this regard. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Yukon talk about the ridicule that was poured on the former government because they had a vision of national development not only for the rest of Canada but particularly for the north.
It was a true vision. It was a vision not only of attracting tourists but of developing resources. That is why the railway and the roads were started, so that we could develop the north as the west was developed. If it had not been for the vision of men like John A. Macdonald in building the railway through the west, and the vision of people like John Diefenbaker in developing the north we would not have the north and we would not have the west and we might even be part of the United States today. Just in case there is any suggestion that I have exaggerated the situation, I want to refer to Hansard for
Supply-Northern Affairs May 11, 1961, page 4673, where the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, had this to say:
I cannot resist the invitation to prolong this discussion for a moment. When the hon. member talks about northern roads-
Here are the words which will be long remembered in the west and by the people of the north.
-whether they are from igloo to igloo or from oil well to oil well or from community to community-
He might have said from oil well to oil well and from mine to mine, because some of the wealthiest mines have been developed in the north. When he ridiculed oil well development, if he did, all I want to say is that it will not be too long before a pipe line will be built from the very area which was ridiculed by this man who had no vision and who criticized the prime minister of that time for his vision. That oil and natural gas resource will be one of the wealthiest resources of Canada.
I say again that I am so happy to see that the minister has not been brainwashed by those Liberals who formerly ridiculed that kind of development, and is now prepared to carry out the Conservative vision of real national development in the north. In fact I must say it is most refreshing. It has made my day for me.

I want to come down out of the clouds to something that is very important to my own riding. It seems funny to talk about these things when you have been on a higher national level, but there are some aggravations in the national parks and we only have the opportunity once a year to discuss them with the minister.
I am not blaming the minister, because he is just one of many ministers who have never been able to prevail over this particular individual in the department who will do nothing in this regard. People come from all over the United States, and the department spends thousands of dollars in advertising Banff park as the most beautiful spot in the world. I agree that it is the most beautiful spot. When these people arrive there many of them get parking tickets-I got one yesterday-for parking in the wrong place. In most cases the first ticket is a warning but in some cases there is a prosecution.
In any city or town in Canada you merely put $1 or $5, depending on where you have parked, in an envelope and send it with the ticket to the officials. But you cannot do that in the parks. This man says no, that such justice would be too quick. In the parks a charge is laid and a great big policeman comes and serves you with a summons. You have got to unpack your suitcases and go back to the motel for another three or four days to await your trial.
This practice has been going on for years. I have dozens of letters. Every minister tells me that something will be done. I have great faith in the present minister. He said to me: I will do this. I got a beautiful letter from him and I wrote Banff and said: "Forget about it; what the Tories would not do the Liberals are going to do for you". Do you know what happened? My friend is clapping. The Liberals have let me down.
The minister has said he will do it as soon as possible. To the people in the park, to say "as soon as possible" is like what the


railway said. They said that it would be developed as soon as possible. That was 1885. The fact is that "as soon as possible" does not mean anything. I do not believe these legal beagles who say you have to amend the act. The minister wags his head. The minister's legal adviser has told him to wag, wag, wag.
The fact is that there have been many unusual orders in council. Let me draw this analogy. We have the order in council that gave Hal Banks a landing permit. I would have thought that would take an act of parliament, but it did not. Surely we could have an order in council in this instance if we are so busy in this place that we cannot amend a little traffic regulation.
As an aside, the federal government says that so far as Hal Banks is concerned they have nothing to do with the matter, but there are two federal men now at Higgins beach, Maine, in the United States. If they are not interested in him, why are they hanging around looking at Hal Banks? That is another question. I must not digress. I just had a telephone call.
I ask the minister seriously to get this other matter into shape because when you charge people like this, whether they are from New York state, Vancouver or some place in Ontario, it is offensive to them.
I want to ask the minister about another matter. I think he should make a clearcut statement on leases. I remember a man by the name of Coleman, director of parks, going to lake Louise. I was there as a member of parliament and I felt so out of place that day. Although I did win the poll in the election I was scared all day because I was treated very unusually on that occasion. I was a Conservative and he was the director. Nevertheless he made them a promise that day without any reservation, and I was quite happy because I figured he would get the ear of the minister, the minister would do something and Eldon Woolliams would be returned to parliament once again. The people were told: You will get a 42 year lease with the right of a 21 year renewal, 63 years. I have piles of letters that have been sent me. I do not want to take all day to read them. The fact is that the people there are frightened about their land tenure. Will the minister tell us if they are going to get leases of this kind?
Because the minister was new in office and did not realize how many votes the Liberals would lose in Banff, he said with a flourish that the government was going to impose a land tax on these people. He has no idea

how much mail I got. Even Mr. Brewster got in touch with my office because he thought the minister had gone off the end a little bit. Mr. Brewster is a very important Liberal in Banff. Seriously speaking, give these people an assurance with regard to their leases. Tell them whether they are going to enjoy land taxes and to what extent. That is what they want to know.
I am not going to say much about expropriation, except that the minister's words are contradicted by the director's actions. A client came into my firm, Woolliams, Kerr and Korman-I am advertising now-and I was not there, but he brought a title in and wanted us to do something about some land. The student went to conduct the search and what do you think was on the title, Mr. Minister? A month or so before these sly little fellows had expropriated the land under some order in council without notifying the client. The minister said this was never done.
This client is a beautiful lady, by the way, and she got a letter. The only reason she got a letter was that the student went down to the registry office and they grabbed the title and said, "That is ours". The student came back and nothing was done until I came home. I phoned the registrar and said, "You have stolen one of our client's titles". He sent it back and written across it was, "expropriated by order in council"-number so and so.
Surely in this country of ours there is still the right of the people to hold land in fee simple. I put this question seriously. I do not own any Canadian Pacific stock, and because I don't I do not criticize the Canadian Pacific. X am a free enterpriser. The Canadian Pacific owns great tracts of land in these parks. If it is all right for the Canadian Pacific to own land in these parks, why is it wrong for anyone else? If you are going to take away all the fee simple land in the park, then let us have no discrimination. I do not know who owns all the stock in the Canadian Pacific. I have read certain lists of stockholders and not all of them are Canadian.
I say to you this: I am not criticizing the Canadian Pacific. They have done a tremendous job in connection with hotels and the service on their trains is far superior to any that is given by any state owned railway.

It is this: In my responsibility as Minister of National Health and Welfare, I was requested by many of his constituents, the people of Calgary and the area who had formed together in a develop-

ment association with a view to that being the site of the winter Olympic games, to go to the Olympic games in Innsbruck last January. At no time before in our history had any representative of the federal government ever shown any interest in the Olympic games by attending. It was the request of that group that caused the Prime Minister to ask me to represent the government at that time.
It was well known to everybody in Calgary who really was interested in the Olympics that no representative of a government could attend at the meeting of the international Olympic association which chooses the site. It was known also that the government could not, because of the international association's rules, make any attempt to influence anyone. Now my hon. friend has sought, by his remarks, to cast aspersions upon me as a representative and indicate I am responsible for this application not being accepted by the international association.
If my hon. friend knows anything at all about the association or about the Olympics, I suggest he contact this group to ascertain that, at their request, the government did everything possible within the Olympic rules. It was only as a result of representations which had been made by other sites and other areas which caused Canada not to be successful. Not only my department, but the department under review, did everything possible.

difficulties about addressing the committee at this point is that that is an awfully difficult act to follow. I say that in the best sense of the word, and I suggest to the hon. lady who was distressed by the speech she just heard that on reading it in Hansard she will find there are many things in it which commend themselves to many members of the treasury benches.
There has been some talk about northern development as it relates to confederation. Twice now I have heard statements by our Prime Minister which distressed me. The first was made in his famous fireside chat when he told the people of this country that Canada is at a crossroads, the crossroads being whether we are going to go on with confederation or go back on it. The second was when the Prime Minister said in the house that the job that faces us in Canada is not nation building but nation saving. Both of these statements are completely wrong. The simple fact of the matter is that 50 per cent of this country is not even in confederation yet.
