I am trying to say that part of the troubles in southern Canada is that those of you who live down here in the south are starting to squabble about all kinds of things that are not really important. You are starting to squabble about language, and quite frankly I am amused when I see the

Supply-Northern Affairs efforts of many people in this chamber, including the Prime Minister, hobbling around on their pidgin French as if this were some kind of contribution.	'

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext: Don't forget John.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
And many others, and the Leader of the Opposition too. It seems to me you are missing the whole problem. You are getting ready to divide the spoils before the country really has anything to divide. Where would southern Canada be today if the early pioneers, who came here by ship and travelled by canoe, had stopped about a quarter of the way west or northwest and began to argue about which language they should use when paddling their canoes or building railways?
This is a great empty country. 1 am not talking now about the Yukon and Northwest Territories alone, although they do have a peculiar shortage of people. I have just finished travelling on the trans-Canada highway from here to Edmonton. This is far south in my terms and I say this land is absolutely empty. We have room for all kinds of people, and I suggest to you if we could somehow or other recapture the great westward and northward push that was characteristic of this country for the first 200 years there were people here, we would be getting over some of our difficulty.
I can tell you that the people of the Yukon and Northwest Territories want to enter confederation at some point, and we are going to enter confederation at some point. We have as much to offer as any other cultural group, any other group from any country overseas, and we are not going to let you people who live down here in the south spoil it for us. We are not going to let you ruin confederation so that there is nothing for us to enter.
I opened my remarks with these statements because one of the basic issues the minister just touched on is the issue of self government for the Yukon and Northwest Territories. The Prime Minister, speaking at the commonwealth conference, made some tremendous statements about how the commonwealth must show leadership and give equality of opportunity, particularly in matters of citizenship, to all peoples. Presumably this was in relation to the Southern Rhodesian question. Because I believed these sentiments as expressed by the Prime Minister I asked a question on orders of the day and I want to know the answer to it now, when we are discussing these estimates. When does the

Prime Minister intend to get on with giving the right to vote to 10,000 Canadian people who live in the north, nearly all of whom are Eskimo people? When are they going to get the right to vote in territorial elections?
It may come as a surprise to people in this country, indeed to most members of parliament, that there are 10,000 people in the Northwest Territories who are not allowed to vote in territorial elections. The council of the Northwest Territories consists of nine members of whom only four are elected. The other five are appointed by the governor in council, in effect by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. The four people who are elected all come from the western part of the Canadian north where there is the concentration of white people, and it is no accident that the only places in the Northwest Territories which have territorial constituencies are those places where there are whites. The granting of territorial franchise to Canadian citizens in the north was something which came about only in response to pressure, and this pressure came invariably only from white people. I do not lay the blame for this situation at the door of any particular administration. All of them are to blame. It has been the fault of the administration generally that it did not think it necessary to give non-white people in northern Canada a vote.
Let me trace the history of these developments. Before 1962, Eskimo people did not enjoy even a federal franchise. It was under the leadership of the then prime minister, who made a categorical commitment in 1959 that another election would not go by in Canada until every Canadian citizen over the age of 21 had the right to vote, that progress was made in this direction. It was in relation to this commitment, and through the medium of the Nielsen bill, that the federal franchise was extended to the Eskimo people of the Canadian north. I want to tell the committee what happened then. For the first time, these people were being consulted in a meaningful way. I refer to the federal election of 1962 which resulted in their having an elected member of parliament.
I may say at this point that the Eskimo people are completely capable in every way of exercising the franchise. Indeed, they showed a lot more responsibility than many Canadians who live in the south, since I believe 79 per cent of them turned out to vote. They began to write to Ottawa on the questions which affected their lives most- matters relating to hunting, trapping, fishing,

education, health and welfare and so on. And the answer they received was that these were territorial matters-that the laws about which they complained, or which they wanted changed, were laws passed by the Northwest Territories council and that these matters should be taken up with their territorial councillors. The immediate reaction on the part of these people was to ask: Who is our territorial councillor? And the answer was: "You do not have one. We have appointed civil servants to the council of the Northwest Territories; we have appointed people who live in Edmonton, Vancouver, and so on-all from southern Canada. We cannot give you the vote in that respect." Mr. Chairman, we gave them the federal franchise-and no one will begrudge it to them-at tremendous cost. But we cannot apparently, create territorial constituencies to give them representatives to whom they may turn directly and who will be accountable to them at the polls.
These people are told, instead: "If you do not like what has been done in terms of territorial legislation, you should see your friendly northern service officer, or see our civil servants. And if you do not like what they are doing, that is too bad." This is exactly what is happening in the Canadian north. As I say, I am not laying the blame on the present minister for this situation, but I say to him that if there was any doubt about whether these 10,000 northern Canadians should have the franchise, surely such a doubt was removed following the 1962 and 1963 federal election campaigns. Surely it was established during those campaigns that it was possible to travel around and visit people- that it was possible for these Eskimo citizens to make a meaningful choice. We know that the Eskimo people are every bit as intelligent as those who live in any constituency in southern Canada one cares to name. I say this: The project upon which the minister must embark before he does anything else in terms of self government is to ensure that these Canadian people have the right to vote in territorial elections. I attend meetings of the Northwest Territories council. We have just finished one. I know how many days are spent by the elected territorial councillors fighting for little things in their own constituencies, bringing to the attention of officials in the department of northern affairs the need for things that are lacking in the constituencies along the Mackenzie river. I know the officials listen sincerely to these representations and take action in accordance
Supply-Northern Affairs with their responsibility to assist these communities. I also know this-and it has been my experience over the years-that in all the council meetings I have attended no one has ever got up to raise his voice on behalf of the Eskimo people of the Keewatin; no one ever raised a problem from a resident in the central Arctic; no one ever said anything about what was going on in the eastern Arctic.
I say to the minister that if 1964 ends before this situation has been rectified, he will have failed. He and his department can figure out new ways of handling parking fines in Banff national park, but if they do not find a way of giving these Canadian people the vote-and it could be done so simply- it were better his administration had never been in office, and better that the department of northern affairs had never existed, because it will only have served to preserve a state of colonialism, after we have received dramatic and graphic proof that these people can handle the vote.
What do the people who live in the Northwest Territories want in terms of a council? We want the right for everybody to vote in territorial elections. That is the first thing. What else do we want? We want a resident commissioner. The executive officer, who in this instance is still a commissioner, should live in the north where we can get at him. We do not want him sitting down in southern Canada, mingling with people from other government agencies and deciding what is good for the people of the north. I do not say this in any disrespectful way. I say it simply as representing a fact of life. If a person lives in Ottawa, he is Ottawa oriented. He does not understand, and regardless of how good his intentions may be, or how well he may be informed, he will not have the trust of the people of the north. We want something else. We want a fully elected council. We are tired of having southern Canadians, particularly senior officers of government, acting as legislators for those of us who live north of the 60th parallel. I have sat in on these meetings, as I have said. People who live in Vancouver, or Edmonton sit around and say: Ho, hum, shall we raise the oil tax in the territories by 4 cents a gallon, or shall we go round the mulberry bush, or shall we have another cup of tea? I am sick and tired of people passing laws when they do not have to live under them. It is a bad principle for any democracy. I am not suggesting that these men are vicious. Far from it. My experience of the appointed members of the council is that without exception they have been fine

Supply-Northern Affairs men who took their responsibilities seriously. But it is not good enough, when people have the right to legislate, that they should take their jobs seriously. It is not good enough to be a benevolent kind of person. If you are not accountable at the polls in Canada for the decisions you make, you have no right to be in any kind of legislative assembly.
How does one bring about the reform to which I have referred? It may sound as though I am asking the minister to make drastic revisions. But he can do it very simply by introducing three minor amendments to the existing Northwest Territories Act in relation to the composition of the council. There shall be nine members, it says right now, four of whom shall be elected from constituencies and five of whom shall be appointed. The hon. gentleman could bring about the situation to which I have referred by simply amending the act so as to say: "The council shall consist of nine members all of whom shall be elected". By making this simple change in the wording of the act the hon. gentleman could give territorial constituencies to all parts of the north, and if he has any doubts about where the boundaries should lie he can get all kinds of help not only from me but from the previous member, the defeated Liberal candidate. Each of us has ample experience of organizing the area. We know it is possible.
The minister has said he is very keen on bringing self government to the territories. He wants to do it. He says he is proceeding fast. I want to repeat an old saying we have in the territories. It is this: You cannot make soup out of caribou tracks. We want more than words from the minister. If, before 1964 expires, he has not introduced into this house some kind of amendment which will give my people the basic democratic right to vote, then I suggest he will have failed.
There is one other matter I should like to bring up, and it relates to what I have been saying.
I have received word today that the department of northern affairs has reduced the relief payable to widows, elderly people and unemployables in the north by $5 a month. They have in some misguided kind of economy measure decided that this is a good way of saving a few thousand dollars. The rates have now been reduced to within 15 cents of the same rate for food allowances for people living in the city of Ottawa. I say this from certain knowledge through consultation. I have here the rates which were reduced in numerous settlements in the Northwest Territories, so I know by how much they were reduced. I

have telephoned the city of Ottawa welfare department and found out that a widow living in Ottawa gets an allowance of $29.15 a month for food, and she has access to supermarkets, the market place, and all that kind of thing. The Eskimo widow living at Baker Lake, which is 350 miles north of Churchill and where food costs are approximately 40 per cent higher than they are at Churchill, Manitoba, gets the same amount.
I would ask the minister, who in the cabinet is responsible for this? Is it the President of the Privy Council, who has been told to make some economies? Did he decide to make this assault on these people? Did he decide that that would be a good spot to save a few dollars? There are only some 2,000 people involved. I know it was not the Minister of National Health and Welfare because I am aware that her department spent $500,000 last year flying out of Eskimo Point, which is a small settlement, some 200 people whose malnutrition and general poor conditions required them to receive hospitalization treatment for t.b. So I know that she did not go to her colleague and tell him to take this $5 away from these Eskimo people. Was it the Minister of Finance, who has never shown any understanding for the people in the north? Before these estimates pass, Mr. Chairman, I want the answer to this, because it is one of the most shameful things which has been done to these Eskimo people for a long time.
I should like to read a letter which I have just received and which caused me to investigate this matter. It was sent by a man who has spent many years in Eskimo country but is no longer with the department of northern affairs. He says, amongst other things:
I gather that all the social assistance basic rates have been radically reduced-just this month- which would constitute a knowing act of assault on the health of the most needy people in the severest part of the nation, where the basic food allowance for an adult was $35 per month-it is now to be only $30-and so on all the way down the scale, ending with the requirement that a five year old child be allowed, presumably, $15 per month for food. Now that original scale was pared down to the bare minimum and anything less than that they know, they bloody well know, is less than even barely enough.
I will be glad to table this letter, Mr. Chairman, because it will be revealing reading to all Canadians.
He goes on to point out he and his wife conducted an experiment. These are people who are well nourished, and had good equipment to cook on. They have cookbooks and know how to save. In this experiment they

attempted to live on $35 a month each for themselves and $15 for the child. They lived like that for one month after the utmost planning. He says that she, his wife, planned the menus for a week ahead knowing what was available in this little community. She figured out the cost. It is a tragic story which he gives of this experiment. He said they did not give up even when they were hungry, and they were hungry all the time that month. Incidentally, this wife pens the note: "The month incidentally was February-the shortest month in the year". Anyway, this is what he says in part:
We failed. Before the end of the month, by which time we were living pretty damn thinly, we were out of a variety of essentials, with theoretically no way of getting them. Despite a lifetime of excellent health and full nutrition, living in a very warm and comfortable house with lots of space, and therefore very little trouble to live hygienically, we were by the end sickly, with colds, running noses, headaches and an increasing feeling of listlessness and weakness. Now, of course, we could have stopped and cheated on the experiment, but we stuck to the assumption that we were relief recipients and kept on with the thing to the end. We knew it would be over at the end of the month and that we did not have to face a lifetime of this.
Now transfer this situation to a man with a t.b. history, who grew up always undernourished, living in a cold, overcrowded house full of equally sickly people, who has lived short of food like this for some time, in the dead of winter when it is near to 60 below-say 85 degrees of frost-with hardly any daylight and in an area where the game is not plentiful at the best of times.
I am not going to read any more of this. I say to the minister, by all means do not throw away money in the Canadian north. No one wants him to do that. I of all people, with my training in the field of social work and with five years experience as an officer in your department, am not anxious to put anyone on relief, and no good social worker is. Save money if you must. But if you want to know how to save money in your department, do not take it away from a handful of miserable people living immediately north of the tree line.
The minister in introducing his estimates said that in the treed country there is wood to burn. At least you have trees and you can build yourself a shelter. But his heart went out to the people living north of the tree line. This is very true. He assessed the situation accurately from his visit, and we know him to be capable of assessing it accurately. But how in God's name does he justify this kind of act by his department in the very area in
Supply-Northern Affairs which he has just told us things are almost impossible for the inhabitants?
If the minister wants to know how to save a few bucks in his department I can tell him how. I would suggest that the first thing he should do is to cancel the plans to go ahead with that multimillion dollar building with air conditioning for the northern affairs staff in the city of Ottawa. If he still needs to save a few more dollars he could cancel the appropriation we have made which runs to many thousands of dollars for field visits by people in Ottawa who go round the north examining this malnutrition which exists there, observing poverty which will be all the worse now that the allowance to these poor wretches has been chopped.
Then there are other ways of saving money. The minister could tighten up the administration of his department. If his field officers -although I doubt this-are passing money out with abandon, then the minister should tighten up. But let him not reduce the relief scale. I also suggest to the minister, in fact I beg him, to reinstate this relief temporarily until we can get the officials of national health and welfare to assess the situation. The Hall commission report has just come in, and I should like to refer to what they said about this. I read this passage into the record the other night, but I will read this damn thing every time I can until this sort of nonsense is stopped. This is a quotation from page 224 of the Hall commission, and this is the situation as it exists today:
"Inhuman"-is the way a public health nurse described, in the course of a conversation, the living conditions of the Eskimos in her community. An apt description indeed. To realize this one has to shed the romantic ideas of Eskimo life, derived from children's books and the movies, and walk through a settlement of Eskimo tents on a cold September night with the wind and rain lashing against the flimsy tents, babies crying and whimpering, and children and adults alike coughing inside.
Surely no one will take this statement I have made this afternoon as any attempt to discredit the minister, because it is not. It is not an attempt to be melodramatic respecting the conditions of the people in this area.
I make it for one reason, and one reason only. I want the minister to go to his officials and say, "Let us suspend implementing this thing until we get the officials of health and welfare, at least, in there", because these officials are invariably ringing the alarm that the health and nutritional levels of the people are still not good enough. On the one hand the minister does this, and on the other hand the department of health and welfare

Supply-Northern Affairs put in the estimates a few hundred thousand dollars to transport sickly people out of that part of the country. Surely we have to stop any further inroads in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit me to deal with this subject, because he has made a statement that our policy has been revised deliberately in order to reduce the amount of relief paid in those areas. I want to tell him that the system upon which relief was paid in those areas was set in 1962 before he became a member of parliament, and it was set by a Conservative government. The reductions which have taken place in this regard are a direct result of the system put into effect in 1962 and are based upon the cost of food only, without regard for other costs in relation to what they were previously. As a result of the reductions, which the hon. member infers are over-all and carte-blanche-which they are not-I am told there are two settlements receiving an increase of $5 a month, 11 settlements have remained unchanged, 14 were reduced by $5 a month, and two were reduced by $10 a month. But this is all related to the basis upon which relief was paid, which was established in 1962.
I will be very glad to look into this situation. I do not think the hon. member is assisting his cause by these terrible stories of conditions up there. He and I know that this sort of thing goes on in cities in southern Canada as well. I do not think it is going to assist the cause of the people there by overemphasizing the seeming degradation. I would ask the hon. member to agree with me that there is not too much degradation there, and among those people in that country there is a tremendous amount of self-preservation and a great deal of happiness, too.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand exactly what the minister is saying. He can do this eggshell dance all day all around this issue, if he wishes to do so. The fact is that conditions in this respect in the Arctic are much worse than they are in the city of Ottawa, for example, and he knows just as sure as he sits there that the cost of living is substantially higher; it is at least 40 per cent higher. I am telling him that the decision to cut these allowances by $5 and $10 a month is unfair; it is unjust, and he cannot stand up in this house and pretend that through some strange formula his officials have arrived at, there is justice in this. I defy the minister to go up into that country and try to survive on the $30 a month that a widow or old person receives. Let him go
[Mr. Rhfiaume.l
to Chesterfield inlet or Pond inlet, for example, and then try to justify what he has said. Is the minister aware that civil servants living in these same areas receive a special ration allowance to compensate for the high cost of living, and this allowance is a lot higher than that received by the people up there?
I am not trying to do the Eskimo a disservice, and I do not want him to do them a disservice either by pretending that somehow or other things are good and we can leave it at that. In 1962 this allowance was established at $35 a month, and the minister says it was written into the plan that it should be lowered at some point, or there was a formula written in. I helped write that damned formula and, no, that was not in there. I do not want the minister to give me this argument that things are pretty tough in the cities, too; because he himself gave the lie to that one when he opened his estimates. He said that conditions under which people have to live north of the tree line are invariably more difficult, and this poses a much more difficult problem for his administration. I know this. I know what the barren lands are like-and so does the minister.
I am not going to belabour this point any more, Mr. Chairman. If the minister insists on going ahead with this reduction I can only say to him that he is making a serious mistake and will be damaging the Eskimo people of these areas-and they are numerous. He suggests that the fact it has not been reduced in 14 communities is some kind of a virtue. Isn't that amazing. I suggest we are going to end up with another item of $500,000 in the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare for transporting people to sanitoria if he does not reconsider this question. I am just asking him to review this matter.
My attention has been drawn to the fact that the cost of living in these areas has gone up and up in the last few months, albeit by only a small amount. I will leave it there, Mr. Chairman. There is no justification for the minister or his officials cutting down this allowance. When I cool off I am going to try to find out which of these ministers has urged this course of action upon him. I am going to do everything I can in this House of Commons to see that when they decide they are going to save $1,000, they are not going to take it away from a group of people who live north of the tree line, who do not have an elected councillor on the Northwest Territories council to fight for them. I, a single member of parliament, am trying to represent

the largest constituency in the free world, with all the attendant problems this brings with it, and I am going to see that somebody speaks for the Eskimos, if the minister abdicates the responsibility given to him by parliament.

Mr. Chairman, the theme of my remarks will be somewhat different from that of the hon. member for Northwest Territories. While we do share together quite a large part of northern Canada, my constituency, though not as large as his, is a large constituency. I have often heard the hon. member for Athabasca refer to the 400 miles of undefended boundary between his constituency and mine. I might say that I share a boundary of some 300 miles with the hon. member for Northwest Territories.
In looking over the estimates, Mr. Chairman, I think of how my constituency has been concerned for a long while about another federal park in that part of Saskatchewan, that vast area where everybody goes for recreation, if they can get there. I might say I was somewhat disappointed to see the reduction in the estimates with regard to campsites and grants to provincial parks, because we were greatly assisted in the provision of roadside tables, and the assistance to provincial parks established by the former government has meant a great deal to that part of Saskatchewan. I was very disappointed to see some curtailment in the cooperation with provincial governments on roadside tables, assistance to provincial parks, winter access roads and so many other things which have meant a great deal to this part of northern Saskatchewan. I have had a great deal of pleasure in working with the departmental officials since coming to Ottawa and I am sure the ones I have talked to are not in favour of the reduction in this assistance which means so much to the people.
With regard to winter access roads, a program instituted by the former government and which meant so much, I wonder whether the minister can tell us if there is going to be greater co-operation with the provinces. The former government ran into difficulty with the socialist government of Saskatchewan with regard to the money we wanted to spend to develop access roads and roads to resources. We always had the stumbling block of the Saskatchewan government saying they must handle the whole thing or nothing would be


done. The federal authorities were not permitted to go in and do it. The construction of winter access roads had to be done through the provincial government and we ran into a lot of stumbling blocks.
I might mention, for instance, the access road to lake La Loche that took so much longer to construct than it should have. So much money was spent by the northern affairs department bringing their equipment in in the fall, taking it out, overhauling it in the winter and taking it back. Hundreds of thousands of dollars were spent in transporting equipment into the job and transporting it out again, but very little work was done. I think this was a shame because there were many private contractors in the area who would have been prepared to move in enough equipment to do the job and we would have got some value for the dollars spent. If we had said we were going to do it some other way the provincial authorities would not have co-operated and consequently nothing would have been done on these winter access roads which mean so much to this part of the country.
We ran into the same thing with regard to roads to resources in Saskatchewan. I think possibly the minister is quite familiar with the very poor progress that was made on the road to Uranium City after the deal was entered into. The route chosen was not the one I would have liked to see followed, but once again the province entered into the picture. After they selected the route and agreed to come in on a 50-50 basis very little was done, for the simple reason the provincial government said they had to do the job. They moved in all their equipment at great expense. Then they found out that they were not road builders and they advocated changing the route to go over to Reindeer lake. These people in the far north have been waiting many years for these roads to resources that were promised them, only to find that now there is a stalemate.
As these estimates progress I wish the minister would tell us what deal the government has made with the new government of Saskatchewan. Has this work been let by contract? Has it been let to private enterprise? Is it on the basis of advertisements for tenders? How is the work progressing on the roads to resources program in Saskatchewan? This is very important.
I should also like to ask the minister whether the road to Uranium City will follow the route first proposed or is it now going to swing off to Reindeer lake, thus for-

getting all about the north? I should also like to hear the minister say something on the plans for winter access roads in northern Saskatchewan. Is it planned to continue the road from La Loche to lake Athabasca and Stony Rapids? These are important matters for the people of my constituency.
I hope that the development programs we started will be continued, that something will be done and that programs will not be handled through the provincial department of natural resources, but that the government will let this work to private contractors by tender and see that it is done. This is one of the obstacles we were up against and I was very happy when, before I entered the political field, the former prime minister came to our area and said they were going to do something for the north and were going to start a program of roads to resources. When I look at the progress which has been made all across Canada I can only say that we have fallen behind in Saskatchewan because we had a government there that did not believe in private enterprise and held up these worth-while projects. These are some of the things I should like the minister to deal with. I should like to know what their plan is and what they propose doing with the continuation of these roads to resources and winter access roads.
I saw some of the most terrible things happen in my constituency this winter. I saw the Department of National Defence send in men to cut the guywires for these radar towers, and let them fall down. I saw these towers topple over. The people of the north could have made use of this equipment, on which the Canadian government has spent millions of dollars, for transformers, radio or television equipment. However, they were allowed to topple over and were sold as scrap. This was done even after the C.B.C. had inquired about these towers and the use which could have been made of them in the north country.
Then, another thing I should like to ask the minister about is the abandonment of the campsite at Gunnar mines. This could mean so much to the north. It is true that Gunnar mines have made so much they do not need to worry about these buildings. The mine has run out of uranium at that point. There are many lovely buildings in this campsite and something could be done with them to assist in northern development. I was wondering if any deal had been entered into with Gunnar mines concerning these buildings, or whether they will be left at this site to deteriorate.
Supply-Northern Affairs These are some of the things that interest the people of the Athabasca region. Certainly, we have a lot of native people in this area. I am sure that many of the buildings in this campsite could be moved on the ice to some of the native settlements and this would make it easier for these people to live. As I say, Gunnar mines are willing to walk away and leave the buildings. Are they going to be left there to be destroyed? Gunnar mines was one of the richest uranium mines in the world, but they have run out of ore and they are willing to pack up and go. I was wondering what is being done about salvaging some of these fine buildings.
I think we have quite a number of tourists going into the north. There are several people that have set up resort areas and fishing camps to which tourists come from a long distance south. I think we should take a good look at this abandoned campsite of Gunnar mines. We should take a good look at what can be salvaged from the radar sites because they could be used to give the people of the area radio and television facilities. These are some of the things that are important to my constituents. I am very much interested in the progress made with access roads and the roads to resources program, as well as the development of our parks. I hope that as the estimates go along the minister will answer some of these questions. As I say, I was very happy to see a program started for development in the north, and I hope it will continue at greater speed than ever.

First of all, I must express my pleasure at seeing you in the chair, sir. I have always thought, particularly in view of the recent announcement that residents of Ottawa may be choosing a mayor, that with the experience you have gained in this kind of role you may consider that line of endeavour. I know that it has only been your great admiration for her performance that has kept you from trying for that position; but that is by the way.
I had hoped to speak about the national museum, which is included in the estimates, but I understand that the Secretary of State and the house leader are going to see that we will have an opportunity, on his estimates,
5974	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs to speak about the national museum. Is my understanding correct? Fine, thank you.
I want to make a remark or two about what was said by the hon. member for Northwest Territories. It is all very well, and I admire him for the strength with which he pushes his representation as a member up there, but like the last speaker I also have a chunk of the north, although it is not as far north. However, it does comprise 148,000 square miles. I have a very large Indian population and a rather small Eskimo population, although I do not get to see them very often. It is very difficult. In the contacts that I have had, particularly with the Indians, and these go back to 193738 when I first got involved in mining, and paddling prospectors around, I have seen nothing to indicate that the Indians in my part of northern Ontario, which is above the track, really feel they have gained anything from the extension of the franchise to them within provincial jurisdiction. As a matter of fact, the interest that they show in it is not particularly keen. I, personally, have sometimes wished that northern affairs was responsible for the Indians in that part of the country rather than the situation that exists at the present time.
It seems to me they would have a better deal if the general administration in the area, in the widest sense, came under northern affairs instead of being broken down between a number of authorities. I should like also to put on the record, not from any party point of view, that I am quite intrigued by the argument made by the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for Northwest Territories on this question of getting provincial status. This is a normal aspiration. I would hope that when the population is larger something like this would really develop. There is nothing that I can see on the horizon to indicate an increase in the population on a scale that would make a provincial organization really justifiable, particularly in economic terms. As I say, it will come and it has to come, but in view of the population, particularly in the Northwest Territories, I do not mind putting on the record that it seems to me this is not feasible or practical at the present tmie.
I am expressing this point of view as an individual member of parliament who is sufficiently interested in the north to read almost everything that comes out in connection with it. I was interested in the book with the very lovely coloured cover that was published not long ago. There is nothing in that book, and there is very little indication


in many of the recent studies that have been published in connection with the north, to indicate that there is going to be some kind of population break-through. It would seem to me that it might be very premature to have a provincial government established when you have such a thin scattering of population over so many points. I have enough experience in my own part of a northern riding to know there is absolutely no connection between Big Trout lake and Lans-downe House. They are both in the north. Big Trout lake is 460 miles north of Port Arthur and the other place, Lansdowne House, is about 420 miles northeast of Port Arthur. They are both in the north. There is absolutely no connection between them, and their lines do not go out to meet at some larger centre. So, you have a problem when you are considering the Northwest Territories, much less the Yukon, because of a situation in which the population is scattered without any kind of nodal point of population having a real influence, that is drawing other communities into their economic orbit or being part of their economic hinterland. It seems to me you have not, as yet, got a condition for a viable province with a provincial economy that has some kind of economic basis that is substantial.
As soon as this begins to really appear it seems to me we would be on our way. I had hoped, as did many other enthusiasts for the north, that Frobisher might be the place, but everyone knows what happened to the dreams and aspirations of that. It is only a few years ago since the hon. member for Qu'Appelle was talking about creating a domed city there, almost like the Houston baseball park, which would have air conditioning and be a model for the world. I was captured by that imaginative glimpse of the future in the Canadian north, but there is a more recent realism that indicates this is some time away.
I hope the hon. members for Yukon and the Northwest Territories will forgive me for getting this far into their territory. I would not want to close without saying I have always noticed in this chamber that the region one comes from is so much more the determinator of performance than the party one belongs to, and I hope the hon. member for Northwest Territories will not mind my saying he reminds we very much of the late Merv Hardy, who also took a very tough and hard line in this chamber so far as the federal agencies working in the north are concerned. I say this to him as a compliment and I hope he will continue being

vigilant and keep giving the minister and the government hell for the inadequacies in the way they treat the people there.
I also want to put on the record a report of a debate which took place here some five years ago. I was reminded of it today because we keep hearing the same speeches over and over again, and this afternoon the hon. member for Bow River gave his annual commercial exploitation in his parks speech. I think it is well for me to put on the record that a number of years ago he also made a fighting, slashing attack on the head hand of bureaucracy that lay over the development of our parks, particularly the ones on the Alberta and B.C. borders. At that time we in the opposition were hooting it up because of his attack on the government of which he was a supporter, but after he had spoken the then minister of northern affairs, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, got up and replied, and according to a report in the Montreal Gazette he said:
I want to make it abundantly clear that I stand for the primary purpose of these parks- the idea that they should be preserved just as they were when the original explorer found them.
It's about time, Mr. Hamilton said, that the millions "who use the parks and love them" band together in an association, free from civil servants and politicians.
How can a minister stand up against the pressures of commercial interests who want to use the parks for mining, forestry and for every honky-tonk recreational device known to man, unless the people who love these parks are prepared to band together and support the minister-?
The report went on to point out that his remarks followed suggestions by a couple of government backbenchers, including the hon. member for Bow River, who suggested that there should be much more commercial enterprise in the parks. It added that the minister said:
If people want to shoot off bullets at a rifle range, or take out electric cars thumping around a circular iron track, or attend open air theatre shows, then I say there are many areas outside the parks which could perfectly well provide such diversion.
I thought it might be just as well to note this because it seems to me the hon. member for Bow River was concentrating this part of his fire on the government as a Liberal government. I think it is worth while noting he also concentrated his fire upon the Conservative government as a Conservative government, on this issue, and the minister at that time stood up to him and issued in effect what I thought was a very effective rebuttal. I would hope the present minister would have the same attitude.
Supply-Northern Affairs
I would like the minister at some time to supply the response that was made to the representations from T. F. Rayner and Judy Rayner of the Marmna development in Jasper, Alberta, where they were developing a ski proposition, and when the matter came up for bid they lost the tender to another organization. They expressed their bitterness over this to a number of members of parliament, since they had a considerable investment in the enterprise not only in the capital sense but in their individual effort, which looked as though it were going down the drain.
I also want to tell the minister I was very surprised when two people in western Canada sent me clippings of a report of a speech he made to the Vancouver real estate board. Each of them was bowled over by certain quotations from his speech, in which he was reported to have said that we could overcome our water shortage by praying for rain. One quotation which was credited to the minister was that if people in the various levels of government would mind their own business we would get along a lot better in this country.
I think that may have been a reporter's paraphrase of his words but it struck me as being unusual and the interpretation put on the minister's words was that everything would be fine in the realm of government if the people in the different jurisdictions would mind their own business. In view of the controversy he has been enmeshed in with the government of Quebec, symbolized by Rene Levesque, this struck me as rather interesting and I wanted to find out more about it.
I sent to the minister's office for a copy of his speech and I was surprised to discover he did not have a text. I do not know whether he spoke without a text, whether he usually free wheels like this, but I was surprised he would appear before such an august body in his own territory and speak without a text, and allow this kind of quotation to appear, which suggested the real solution to the difficulties of the country was to have politicians at certain levels of government to mind their own business.
I would be very interested in hearing from the minister that he did not have a text of his speech. I know the former prime minister, the Leader of the Opposition, had a great reputation for speaking off the cuff, but one of the things that always intrigued me was when you wrote to his office they could always send you a text.

Well, this is very true but sometimes, Mr. Chairman, we used to get from the right hon. gentleman's office the text of a speech that was prepared and never given, because of the hon. gentleman's ability to ad lib and take off from his text. I do not think he would be one to deny that. But this practice of the minister, as exemplified by his speech to the Vancouver real estate board, interested me because, as I say, it fitted in with the Quebec controversy, and also took me back to that stirring announcement he made not too many months ago about that magnificent scholarship scheme. There is a text of that speech, I understand, and it certainly raised many hopes. We all remember the magnificent Toronto Star head-fine and we wondered what the minister of northern affairs was doing in this particular field, offering these 10,000 scholarships-come and get them, all you need is your talent.
I hope the minister can gather from these remarks that I and some of my colleagues are interested in his performance in almost every way. We have been intrigued with his relations with the premier of Saskatchewan. I understand the premier of Saskatchewan feels he has only one soulmate in the federal cabinet and that is the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I do not know the premier of Saskatchewan very well, but it rather surprised me that he would prefer the minister of northern affairs to the Minister of Trade and Commerce as his liaison, his interlocutor, with the stalwarts in the Pearson cabinet.
Naturally there is a tendency among those of us who are somewhat suspicious of the motives and intent of the premier of Saskatchewan to transfer this suspicion to the minister of northern affairs, as his buddy. I realize this may be unfair of us. In the same way, I sometimes transfer some of my annoyance with the hon. member for Kootenay West to the hon. member for Kootenay East, and if the minister could do anything to straighten us out as to his attachment to the premier of Saskatchewan I think we would all be interested to hear him.
I wish to ask the minister a question now, relating to the salary scales applicable to


teachers within his department. These were recently increased, and I have had placed on the record through questions this session the figures for all the various government agencies which employ teachers. There is no question in my mind but that salaries paid to teachers in this department compare very favourably with those paid by other departments of government. I am not against this, but I should like to know what the governing factors are. The minister will remember that the Glassco commission report was not so flattering to the teaching effort of the department of northern affairs as it was to that of the Indian affairs branch. If I may paraphrase the report of the royal commission in this respect, it is that they were doubtful about the value we are getting for the money spent on education by this department particularly as compared with the Indian affairs branch. I was bothered by this because I have not been much impressed by the value we have been getting out of the schools run by the Indian affairs branch, and consequently I wondered what standards of efficiency were being used. While the Indian affairs branch may be able to do the work cheaper than the department of northern affairs, I am also very much aware that the standard of some of the teachers is not as high as the standard of those employed by the department of northern affairs. If the minister can show me that part of the higher cost of teachers in his department is a consequence of achieving a higher standard of teaching than in comparable government departments, I would be most interested. I have often thought, in the light of the response which the Department of National Defence has achieved in getting teachers for Canadian children in Europe by paying the salaries of the teachers to the school boards in the areas from which they come, that a similar arrangement might well be established in the hon. gentleman's department. It seems to me there is a discontinuity in the teaching of classes, both in the department of northern affairs and in the Indian affairs branch, because it is found difficult to obtain the services of teachers for any length of time, and I should like to suggest that it might be possible, particularly because of the romantic aura which would surround teaching for a year or two in the north, to change completely the teacher recruitment practice which now exists and, for the staffing of northern schools, rely on a policy of the kind followed by the Department of National Defence.

I appreciate that this might be more expensive. I can think, for example, of teachers employed by the board of education of Kapus-kasing, which probably pays the highest salaries in Ontario, going over to teach in Europe and enjoying a salary as high as any paid by the department of northern affairs. On the other hand, one can be almost certain of getting high quality and I am confident that the quality of the teaching in our schools in Europe as a result of the policy adopted by the Department of National Defence is exceptionally high. I think it is above the national standard. In the visits I have made to those schools, as a result of conversations with the teachers I was very much taken by the quality of the staff, and I believe this same quality might be achieved if there were an imaginative recruitment scheme using the services of teachers on loan from schools in southern Canada for a year or two. It may be objected that something would be lost because teachers would not be in the north for a long time and would not become acclimatized to conditions there. I would argue that a classroom, whether in southern Ontario or West Germany or the far north, is much the same. It is the other conditions which change. I suggest that the turnover in the schools in the minister's department is already such that if we could get teachers to undertake a northern assignment for two years there would be just as much continuity as exists at the present time.
I do not wish to close without adding a comment to the minister's own comment about his good relations with, and the good work he got out of, his parliamentary secretary. I often feel that these humble people are not given sufficient recognition, particularly by the opposition. It is rarely that we find a minister prepared to hold up his follower as an exemplar-as someone who is on his way and who is going somewhere. We felt, ever since we got to hear about this particular hon. member, when he made headlines right across the country through his dancing ability, that he would go far in Canadian politics and we welcome this recognition of this new kind of dancing which has caught on with the minister.
Item stands.
